stem: Your MCP server offers three things: (1) a `send_message` action, (2) read-only database schemas for context, and (3) a "Summarize my meetings" template users pick from a slash-command menu. Which MCP building blocks are these?

choices.text: (1) Resource, (2) Tool, (3) Prompt
choices.reason: Swapped: actions the model calls are tools; passive read-only data is a resource.

choices.text: (1) Tool, (2) Resource, (3) Prompt
choices.reason: Correct: tools are functions the model calls, resources are passive read-only data, prompts are user-invoked templates.

choices.text: (1) Tool, (2) Prompt, (3) Resource
choices.reason: Schemas are passive data (a resource); a reusable template the user invokes is a prompt.

choices.text: All three are tools, since the model uses each of them
choices.reason: MCP has three distinct building blocks, each with a different controller: model, application or user.

takeaway: **Tools** = model-controlled actions, **Resources** = application-controlled read-only context, **Prompts** = user-invoked templates.
explanation: Each MCP building block is defined by **who controls it**. Tools are functions the model calls, so `send_message` is a tool. Resources are passive read-only data the application provides, so database schemas are a resource. Prompts are templates the user invokes, like a slash-command menu item, so the meeting template is a prompt (Option B). A is the tempting trap because it swaps tools and resources, and C swaps resources and prompts. D ignores that MCP has three distinct primitives with different controllers.
mnemonic: Tools: model. Resources: app. Prompts: user.

stem: Your agent has 12 tools, each with a one-line description such as "Gets data." Claude often picks the wrong tool or misuses parameters. Following Anthropic's guidance on defining tools, what should you change first?

choices.text: Split each tool into several narrower tools, one per action, so each name explains itself
choices.reason: The guidance is the opposite: consolidate related operations into fewer tools, which reduces selection ambiguity.

choices.text: Shorten the names and drop the descriptions so the tool definitions cost fewer tokens
choices.reason: Descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance; the more context Claude has, the better it decides when and how to use each tool.

choices.text: Write fuller descriptions: what each tool does, when to use it, its parameters and caveats
choices.reason: Correct: detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance. Aim for at least 3–4 sentences per tool.

choices.text: Add `input_examples` to every tool instead of writing descriptions, since examples show usage
choices.reason: Clear descriptions are most important; `input_examples` are an optional extra for complex, nested or format-sensitive inputs.

takeaway: Tool quality starts with the **description**: what it does, when (and when not) to use it, each parameter, and caveats.
explanation: Anthropic's guidance says detailed **descriptions** are by far the most important factor in tool performance. One-line text like 'Gets data.' leaves Claude guessing, so write what each tool does, when to use it, its parameters and caveats, aiming for at least 3–4 sentences per tool (Option C). D is the tempting trap because examples show usage, but `input_examples` are an optional extra for complex inputs, not a replacement. A goes against the advice to consolidate related operations, and B removes exactly the context Claude needs.

stem: On a model that supports forced tool use, you want every response to call your `record_summary` tool: never a different tool, and never a plain-text answer. Which `tool_choice` fits?

choices.text: `{"type": "tool", "name": "record_summary"}`
choices.reason: Correct: `tool` forces Claude to always use that particular tool.

choices.text: `{"type": "any"}`, so every response has to call a tool
choices.reason: `any` tells Claude it must use one of the provided tools, but it doesn't force a particular tool.

choices.text: `{"type": "auto"}`, the default whenever tools are provided
choices.reason: `auto`, the default when tools are provided, lets Claude decide whether to call any tool at all.

choices.text: `{"type": "none"}`, with `record_summary` as the only tool
choices.reason: `none` prevents Claude from using any tools.

takeaway: **auto**: Claude decides. **any**: some tool. **tool**: this tool. **none**: no tools.
explanation: Each `tool_choice` type sets a different level of control: `auto` lets Claude decide, `any` requires some tool, `tool` forces one specific tool, and `none` blocks tools. The stem wants `record_summary` every time, never another tool and never plain text, so only `{"type": "tool", "name": "record_summary"}` fits (Option A). B is the tempting trap because it does force a tool call, but it allows any of the provided tools. C leaves the choice to Claude, and D prevents tool use entirely.
mnemonic: Auto decides, any picks, tool insists, none forbids.

stem: Claude returns three `tool_use` blocks in one response. Your code runs them and sends each `tool_result` back in its own user message. As the conversation goes on, Claude stops making parallel calls. What's wrong?

choices.text: Parallel calls are off by default; set `disable_parallel_tool_use: false`
choices.reason: Parallel tool use is on by default; `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` is only for turning it off.

choices.text: All three results belong together in one user message, before any text
choices.reason: Correct: a separate user message per result is the most common formatting mistake, and it "teaches" Claude to avoid parallel calls.

choices.text: The tools must run concurrently, or Claude treats the calls as sequential
choices.reason: The API doesn't prescribe an execution order: concurrent, sequential or a mix is your choice.

choices.text: The results must be sent in the same order as the `tool_use` blocks
choices.reason: Each result is matched to its call by `tool_use_id`; the problem here is splitting the results across messages.

takeaway: Parallel calls need **one** user message holding every `tool_result`, results first and any text after.
explanation: When Claude makes several `tool_use` calls in one response, all their `tool_result` blocks belong in **one** user message, before any text. Sending each result in its own message is the most common formatting mistake, and it 'teaches' Claude to avoid parallel calls, which matches the symptom (Option B). D is the tempting trap because ordering seems important, but each result is matched by `tool_use_id`. A is wrong because parallel tool use is on by default, and C wrongly assumes the API prescribes execution order.

diagram.caption: Keep every result in a single user message so parallelism keeps working.

stem: Claude sends three dependent `tool_use` blocks in one turn. You run them in order, the first one fails, and you skip the other two. What should your next user message contain?

choices.text: A `tool_result` per call: the failure, plus `is_error: true` and a brief note for skipped ones
choices.reason: Correct: return one `tool_result` for each `tool_use` block. For a call you chose not to run, send `is_error: true` and a brief explanation.

choices.text: Only the failed call's `tool_result`; calls you skipped never ran, so they need nothing
choices.reason: Every `tool_use` block needs its own `tool_result`, including calls you chose not to run.

choices.text: A plain text message explaining the failure and the skipped calls, with no `tool_result` blocks
choices.reason: Results go back as `tool_result` blocks matched by `tool_use_id`, and they come before any text in the message.

choices.text: Nothing yet; rerun the whole batch yourself until it succeeds, then send all three results
choices.reason: The documented pattern is to return `is_error: true` results; Claude can then reissue calls on the next turn.

takeaway: Every `tool_use` gets a `tool_result`, even calls you skipped: mark those `is_error: true` and say why.
explanation: The rule is that **every** `tool_use` block gets a `tool_result`, including calls you chose not to run. Send the failure for the first call, and for each skipped one return `is_error: true` with a brief explanation, which is Option A; Claude can then reissue calls on the next turn. B is the tempting trap because skipped calls never ran, but they still need results. C drops the `tool_result` blocks entirely, and D replaces the documented error-result pattern with your own retries.

stem: Your request enables `web_search`, Anthropic's `bash` tool and your own `get_inventory` tool. Which of them must your application execute and answer with `tool_result` blocks?

choices.text: Only `get_inventory`, because Anthropic defines and maintains the other two
choices.reason: Anthropic publishes the `bash` schema, but it's client-executed: your application runs each call and returns the result.

choices.text: All three, because the model never executes anything itself
choices.reason: The model doesn't, but Anthropic's servers run server tools like `web_search`; you never construct a `tool_result` for them.

choices.text: None of them; Claude runs every tool listed in `tools`
choices.reason: Only server tools run on Anthropic's infrastructure. User-defined and Anthropic-schema tools run in your application.

choices.text: `bash` and `get_inventory`; `web_search` runs on Anthropic's servers
choices.reason: Correct: tools differ by where the code executes. Both client tools run in your application; the server tool runs on Anthropic's infrastructure.

takeaway: Ask **where the code runs**: user-defined and Anthropic-schema tools are yours to execute; server tools are Anthropic's.
explanation: Ask **where the code runs**. Server tools such as `web_search` run on Anthropic's infrastructure, so you never build a `tool_result` for them. User-defined tools like `get_inventory` and Anthropic-schema tools like `bash` are client-executed: your application runs each call and returns the result, so the answer is D. A is the tempting trap because Anthropic publishes the `bash` schema, but publishing a schema doesn't mean Anthropic executes it. B wrongly includes the server tool, and C wrongly assumes Claude runs everything listed.

stem: Your support agent uses the SDK tool runner. You're adding an `issue_refund` tool, and a person must approve each refund before it runs. What does Anthropic's tool runner page recommend?

choices.text: Keep the tool runner, since it already asks before running each of the tool calls
choices.reason: The tool runner runs tools automatically when Claude calls them and sends the results back; it doesn't wait for a person.

choices.text: Set `max_iterations` to 1 so that at most one refund can happen per run
choices.reason: `max_iterations` only caps how many times the runner loops; it adds no approval step.

choices.text: Write the manual tool-use loop, so your code can pause for approval first
choices.reason: Correct: the page says to use the manual loop when you need human-in-the-loop approval, custom logging or conditional execution.

choices.text: Call `runner.until_done()` and review the final message before replying
choices.reason: `until_done()` returns the final message after the runner has already run the tools, too late to approve a refund.

takeaway: Risky tool that needs a human yes? Drive the loop yourself; the tool runner executes tools automatically.
explanation: The SDK tool runner executes tools **automatically** when Claude calls them and sends the results back, so it has no point where a person can approve a refund. The tool runner page says to write the manual tool-use loop when you need human-in-the-loop approval, custom logging or conditional execution (Option C). A is the tempting trap because it assumes the runner already asks first. B only caps loop iterations, and D returns the final message after the tools have already run.

stem: Your Python MCP server uses the stdio transport. After you add `print()` calls for debugging, the server breaks and the client can't talk to it reliably. What should you do?

choices.text: Log with the `logging` module, which writes to stderr, and drop `print()`
choices.reason: Correct: never write to stdout in a stdio server. The standard `logging` module writes to stderr, so the JSON-RPC messages stay intact.

choices.text: Flush stdout after every `print()` call so the debug lines don't interleave
choices.reason: Writing to stdout at all corrupts the JSON-RPC messages; `print()` writes to stdout by default, flushed or not.

choices.text: Prefix each debug line with `#` so the client knows to skip those lines
choices.reason: In a stdio server, anything written to stdout corrupts the JSON-RPC messages, however it's marked.

choices.text: Remove all logging, since MCP servers have no safe channel for logs
choices.reason: Servers can log: the guide recommends the standard `logging` module, with one logger per module.

takeaway: In a stdio server, **stdout carries the protocol**: send logs to stderr. HTTP servers can log to stdout.
explanation: In a stdio MCP server, **stdout carries the protocol**: anything written there corrupts the JSON-RPC messages. `print()` writes to stdout by default, which is why the server broke. The standard `logging` module writes to stderr, so switching to it keeps messages intact (Option A). B is the tempting trap because interleaving looks like the problem, but writing to stdout at all corrupts the stream, flushed or not. C's markers don't help for the same reason, and D is wrong because servers can log safely to stderr.
mnemonic: stdout for messages, stderr for logs.

stem: Your team's MCP server runs locally over stdio and exposes tools and resources. You want a Messages API backend to use it through the MCP connector. What has to change?

choices.text: Nothing; put the server's stdio launch command in the `mcp_servers` entry
choices.reason: An `mcp_servers` entry takes `type: "url"` and an https URL, and local stdio servers can't be connected directly.

choices.text: Pass an `authorization_token` so the API can reach the server on your machine
choices.reason: `authorization_token` is an OAuth token for servers that require one; it doesn't make a local stdio server reachable.

choices.text: Expose it over HTTP at a publicly reachable https URL
choices.reason: Correct: the connector reaches servers over HTTP at a public URL; local stdio servers can't be connected directly.

choices.text: List its resources in the `mcp_toolset` so Claude can read them as context
choices.reason: An MCP toolset configures which of the server's tools are enabled; it doesn't make a local server reachable.

takeaway: The MCP connector needs a **public HTTP** server; local stdio servers can't connect directly.
explanation: The MCP connector calls remote servers for you, so the server must be **publicly exposed over HTTP** (`type: "url"` with an https URL). A local stdio server therefore has to be exposed at a public https URL (C). A hopes the launch command works as-is, but local stdio servers can't be connected directly. B's `authorization_token` is for OAuth, and D's toolset only configures which tools are enabled.

diagram.caption: The connector reaches remote servers only; local stdio servers can't connect directly.

stem: A team wants to install 30 Skills, each with a long SKILL.md, reference files and scripts, but worries they will fill the context window on every request. What loads into context before a Skill is triggered?

choices.text: Every Skill's full SKILL.md body, so Claude can choose between them well
choices.reason: The SKILL.md body loads only when a request matches the Skill's description.

choices.text: Everything, including reference files and script code
choices.reason: Bundled files load only when read, and scripts run through bash: only their output enters context.

choices.text: Nothing; Claude finds a Skill only when you name it
choices.reason: Metadata is always loaded at startup and included in the system prompt, so Claude can use Skills automatically.

choices.text: Only each Skill's `name` and `description` metadata
choices.reason: Correct: with progressive disclosure, only Level 1 metadata occupies context until a Skill is triggered.

takeaway: Skills load in stages: **metadata always**, the SKILL.md body when triggered, files and script output only as needed.
explanation: Skills use **progressive disclosure**, loading in stages. At startup only each Skill's `name` and `description` sits in context; the SKILL.md body loads when a request matches, and files and script output load only as needed (D). A is the tempting trap because choosing between Skills seems to require their full bodies, but the description is what Claude matches. B overstates what loads, and C is wrong because metadata is always loaded so Claude can use Skills automatically.

diagram.caption: Progressive disclosure: each level loads only when it's needed.

stem: Your custom Skill's frontmatter says `description: Invoice helper`. Its SKILL.md body explains that it should be used whenever a user uploads an invoice, yet Claude rarely uses it. What's the fix?

choices.text: Rename it `claude-invoice-helper` so its name stands out to Claude
choices.reason: A Skill name can't contain the reserved word "claude", and Claude matches requests against the description.

choices.text: Rewrite the `description` to say what the Skill does and when to use it
choices.reason: Correct: the description is what Claude matches your request against, so it must say both what the Skill does and when to use it.

choices.text: Move more of the trigger details into the SKILL.md body, where Claude reads them
choices.reason: The body enters context only after the Skill is triggered, so trigger details there can't help Claude decide.

choices.text: Paste the Skill's instructions into every user prompt
choices.reason: Skills load on demand precisely so you don't have to repeat the same guidance across conversations.

takeaway: A Skill is triggered by its **description**: state what it does and when to use it.
explanation: Claude decides whether to use a Skill by matching the request against its **`description`**. 'Invoice helper' says neither what the Skill does nor when to use it, so rewrite the description to say both (Option B). C is the tempting trap because the trigger details are already in the body, but the body enters context only after the Skill is triggered, too late to help Claude decide. A uses the reserved word 'claude' and targets the name, and D defeats the point of loading Skills on demand.

stem: In Claude Code, a side investigation reads dozens of files and produces output you won't reference again, and your main conversation's context keeps filling up. Which extension fits best?

choices.text: A subagent, which works in its own context and returns a summary
choices.reason: Correct: subagents give context isolation. The work happens separately and only a summary returns to your conversation.

choices.text: Put the investigation steps in CLAUDE.md so they're always available
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md loads in full every session, so it adds context rather than isolating the work.

choices.text: A hook that runs the investigation after every edit
choices.reason: Hooks fire on lifecycle events for automation that must run every time; workflows that need reasoning suit skills.

choices.text: An MCP server that runs the investigation as an external tool
choices.reason: MCP connects Claude to external services and data; it doesn't isolate work from your conversation.

takeaway: A side task floods your context? Route it through a **subagent**: only its summary comes back.
explanation: The clue is a side investigation whose output you **won't reference again**, filling your main context. Subagents give context isolation: the work happens in their own context and only a summary returns, which is Option A. D is the tempting trap because an MCP server feels external, but MCP connects Claude to outside services and data; it doesn't isolate work. B adds to every session's context instead of isolating it, and C fires on lifecycle events for automation, not for a reasoning task.

stem: After running a client tool, your app sends a user message whose content is a text block, "Here are the results:", followed by the `tool_result` block. The API returns a 400 error. What fixes it?

choices.text: Send the text in its own user message first, then the `tool_result` in a second message
choices.reason: Tool results must immediately follow their tool use blocks: you can't include any messages between the assistant's tool use message and the tool result message.

choices.text: Put the `tool_result` block first in the content array, with any text after it
choices.reason: Correct: in the user message holding tool results, `tool_result` blocks must come first in the content array; any text must come after all of them.

choices.text: Send the result in a message with a `tool` role, the way other function-calling APIs do
choices.reason: Unlike APIs with special `tool` or `function` roles, the Claude API carries `tool_result` blocks inside ordinary `user` messages.

choices.text: Add `is_error: false` to the `tool_result` so the API accepts text placed before it
choices.reason: `is_error` only signals that the tool failed. The 400 comes from the ordering: text before a `tool_result` is rejected.

takeaway: In a tool-result message, `tool_result` blocks go **first**; any text comes after them.
explanation: In a user message that carries tool results, the `tool_result` blocks must come **first** in the content array, with any text after all of them. Putting 'Here are the results:' before the result is what triggers the 400, so reorder the blocks (Option B). A is the tempting trap because separating the text seems clean, but tool results must immediately follow their tool use blocks, with no messages between. C uses a `tool` role the Claude API doesn't have, and D's `is_error` only signals tool failure.

stem: During development, Claude often calls your `create_ticket` tool with a required parameter missing. Returning an `is_error` result lets it recover, but you want these invalid calls to stop happening in the first place. Which changes does Anthropic's guide point to?

choices.text: Return an `is_error` result naming the missing parameter, so Claude retries with it filled in
choices.reason: That's recovery, not prevention: given an error result, Claude retries 2-3 times with corrections, but the invalid call has already happened.

choices.text: Write more detailed `description` values for the tool and its parameters
choices.reason: Correct: an invalid call usually means Claude lacked enough information; the docs' best bet during development is more-detailed `description` values.

choices.text: Resend the same request unchanged until Claude includes the missing parameter
choices.reason: An invalid call usually means Claude didn't have enough information; resending the same request adds none, so the mistake can repeat.

choices.text: Shorten the parameter descriptions so the schema is quicker for Claude to follow
choices.reason: This removes the information Claude lacks. The guide points the other way: more-detailed `description` values in your tool definitions.

choices.text: Set `strict: true` on the tool definition
choices.reason: Correct: strict tool use guarantees tool inputs always match your schema exactly, preventing missing parameters and type mismatches.

takeaway: Prevent bad tool calls with **richer descriptions** and `strict: true`; `is_error` results only help Claude recover.
explanation: The stem asks to **prevent** invalid calls, not recover from them. An invalid call usually means Claude lacked information, so more-detailed `description` values for the tool and its parameters address the cause (B). Setting `strict: true` guarantees tool inputs always match your schema, preventing missing parameters (E). A is the most tempting wrong pick because returning `is_error` does help, but it is recovery after the invalid call already happened. C adds no information, and D removes it.

stem: Your app enables Anthropic's `web_search` tool alongside your own `lookup_order` tool, and you're adding error handling. For which tool must your code send `tool_result` blocks with `is_error: true` when something fails?

choices.text: Only `lookup_order`; Claude itself handles errors from server tools like `web_search`
choices.reason: Correct: you return client tool errors with `is_error: true`. Claude handles server tool errors transparently, so you don't handle `is_error` results for them.

choices.text: Both of them, because every failed tool call needs an `is_error` result from your code
choices.reason: Unlike client tools, you do not need to handle `is_error` results for server tools such as web search; Claude handles those errors transparently.

choices.text: Only `web_search`, because errors from Anthropic's own tools must be acknowledged by you
choices.reason: It's the reverse: server tool errors (like `too_many_requests` for web search) are Claude's to handle; your own tool's failures are yours to report.

choices.text: Neither of them; the API detects every tool failure and retries the failed call by itself
choices.reason: Your code runs `lookup_order`, so only your code knows it failed: return the error in `content` with `is_error: true`.

takeaway: `is_error` is for **your** tools' failures; server tool errors are handled by Claude without your code.
explanation: The split follows **who runs the tool**. Your code runs `lookup_order`, so only your code knows it failed and must return the error with `is_error: true`. Server tools like `web_search` run on Anthropic's side, and Claude handles their errors transparently, so you don't send `is_error` results for them (Option A). B is the tempting trap because it treats every tool alike. C reverses the responsibility, and D wrongly assumes the API detects your own tool's failures.

stem: Your API agent sends about 200 tool definitions from GitHub, Slack, Sentry and other services on every request. They cost tens of thousands of tokens before any work starts, and Claude increasingly picks the wrong tool. Which approach does Anthropic document for this?

choices.text: Split the catalog across separate requests, sending about 50 tool definitions in each
choices.reason: Claude's tool selection accuracy degrades once you exceed 30–50 available tools, so 50 per request is still where it starts to slip.

choices.text: Cut every tool description down to one line so all 200 definitions fit in fewer tokens
choices.reason: Shorter descriptions still load every definition up front; the documented fix loads only the 3–5 tools a given request needs.

choices.text: Set `defer_loading: true` on every tool, including the tool search tool itself
choices.reason: At least one tool, normally the tool search tool itself, must stay non-deferred.

choices.text: Add the tool search tool and set `defer_loading: true` on tools not needed up front
choices.reason: Correct: Claude searches the catalog and loads only what it needs, typically cutting definition tokens by over 85% while selection accuracy stays high.

takeaway: Hundreds of tools? Add **tool search** with `defer_loading: true`; selection accuracy degrades past 30–50 loaded tools.
explanation: Sending ~200 tool definitions costs tokens up front, and selection accuracy degrades once you exceed 30–50 available tools. The documented fix is the **tool search tool** with `defer_loading: true` on tools not needed up front, so Claude loads only what each request needs (Option D). A is the tempting trap because splitting looks like it solves size, but 50 per request is still where accuracy starts to slip. B still loads every definition, and C defers the search tool itself, which must stay non-deferred.

stem: You're wrapping an address-book API for an agent. Your first tool, `list_contacts`, returns every contact, just like the API's main endpoint. The agent wastes context reading thousands of entries to find one person. What does Anthropic's post on writing tools for agents suggest?

choices.text: Keep `list_contacts` and tell the agent in its system prompt to scan the results carefully
choices.reason: Reading every contact token by token is the brute-force search the post warns about; better instructions don't stop the list from filling context.

choices.text: Replace it with a targeted tool such as `search_contacts` that finds the relevant person
choices.reason: Correct: the post suggests implementing `search_contacts` or `message_contact` instead of `list_contacts`, so the agent skips to the relevant entry.

choices.text: Wrap every endpoint of the API as its own tool, so the agent has the most flexibility
choices.reason: The post calls tools that merely wrap existing API endpoints a common error: more tools don't always lead to better outcomes.

choices.text: Return the contacts as compact JSON, so the full list costs fewer tokens to read through
choices.reason: A compact list still sends every contact into the agent's limited context; the post's fix is a tool built for the workflow.

takeaway: Design tools around the agent's workflow (`search_contacts`), not around raw endpoints (`list_contacts`).
explanation: Anthropic's post on writing tools says to design tools around the **agent's workflow**, not around raw API endpoints. A `list_contacts` tool forces the agent into brute-force reading of every entry, so a targeted `search_contacts` tool that finds the relevant person fits (Option B). D is the tempting trap because a compact format cuts tokens, but every contact still lands in the agent's limited context. A relies on instructions that don't shrink the list, and C repeats the endpoint-wrapping error the post warns about.

source.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents

stem: Your `find_documents` tool returns each match as a UUID, a `mime_type` and a `256px_image_url`. The agent often cites the wrong document and sometimes invents IDs. Some follow-up tools still need the UUIDs. What does Anthropic's post on writing tools recommend?

choices.text: Return names and readable fields, with a `response_format` option to include IDs when needed
choices.reason: Correct: resolving UUIDs to meaningful language reduces hallucinations, and a `concise`/`detailed` `response_format` enum lets the agent get IDs for follow-up calls.

choices.text: Return the full raw API record for every match, so the agent has each field it could ever need
choices.reason: The post says to return only high-signal information and prioritize contextual relevance over flexibility; raw records add fields like `mime_type`.

choices.text: Keep the UUIDs but sort them alphabetically, so the agent can keep track of them more easily
choices.reason: Sorting doesn't help: the post found that resolving arbitrary alphanumeric UUIDs to meaningful language is what improves precision.

choices.text: Remove the follow-up tools that need UUIDs, so responses never have to include any IDs
choices.reason: The post's `search_user` → `send_message(id=...)` example shows agents may still need IDs; a `response_format` enum keeps both options.

takeaway: Return **meaningful** names, not cryptic IDs; let a `response_format` parameter add IDs when a later call needs them.
explanation: The post recommends returning **meaningful** language over cryptic identifiers, because resolving UUIDs to names reduces hallucinations. Since some follow-up tools still need the UUIDs, a `response_format` enum such as `concise`/`detailed` lets the agent request IDs when needed, which is Option A. D is the tempting trap because it removes IDs entirely, but agents may still need them for follow-up calls. B adds low-signal fields like `mime_type`, and C's sorting doesn't make UUIDs meaningful.

stem: Your IDE acts as an MCP host and connects to three MCP servers: a local filesystem server, a GitHub server and a remote Sentry server. How does MCP structure these connections?

choices.text: One shared MCP client in the IDE multiplexes all three servers over a single connection
choices.reason: The host creates one MCP client for each MCP server; there's no single client shared across servers.

choices.text: The host creates one MCP client per server, each keeping its own dedicated connection
choices.reason: Correct: an MCP host creates one MCP client for each MCP server, and each client maintains a dedicated connection with its server.

choices.text: Each server runs its own MCP client that connects back to the IDE to deliver context
choices.reason: It's the other way round: clients live in the host and obtain context from servers, the programs that provide context to clients.

choices.text: The three servers federate into one combined server, and the IDE talks only to that one
choices.reason: The host coordinates multiple clients, one per server; the servers stay separate programs that run locally or remotely.

takeaway: **Host** = the AI app; it creates **one client per server**; each **server** provides context to its client.
explanation: MCP's architecture has three roles: the **host** is the AI application, it creates **one MCP client per server**, and each client keeps its own dedicated connection to that server. So the IDE creates three clients, one per server, which is Option B. A is the tempting trap because one shared client sounds efficient, but MCP has no client shared across servers. C reverses the roles, since clients live in the host and obtain context from servers, and D invents a federation step that doesn't exist.

stem: Your company wants a single MCP server for its ticketing system that hundreds of employees' AI apps can connect to over the network. Which transport fits?

choices.text: stdio, since it gives optimal performance with no network overhead
choices.reason: stdio is for local processes on the same machine; its no-overhead benefit doesn't help clients across the network.

choices.text: stdio, with each employee's app pointed at the server's network address
choices.reason: stdio uses standard input/output streams between local processes; there's no network address for remote apps to connect to.

choices.text: Streamable HTTP, which enables remote servers that serve many clients
choices.reason: Correct: Streamable HTTP enables remote server communication, and remote servers using it typically serve many MCP clients.

choices.text: Either one, since a stdio server handles remote clients the same way
choices.reason: Local stdio servers typically serve a single MCP client; remote servers using Streamable HTTP typically serve many.

takeaway: **stdio** = local, usually one client. **Streamable HTTP** = remote, many clients, standard HTTP auth (OAuth recommended).
explanation: The key details are **over the network** and **hundreds of employees**. Streamable HTTP enables remote server communication, and remote servers using it typically serve many MCP clients, which is Option C. A is the tempting trap because stdio's no-overhead performance sounds attractive, but stdio is for local processes on the same machine. B is wrong because stdio uses input/output streams with no network address, and D ignores that local stdio servers typically serve a single client.

stem: Your MCP server's `book_room` tool receives a date in the wrong format. You want the model to notice and retry with a corrected date. How should the server report the problem?

choices.text: As a JSON-RPC protocol error, the standard channel for any bad tool input
choices.reason: Protocol errors are for unknown tools, malformed requests and server errors, and models are less likely to recover from them.

choices.text: In the tool result, with `isError: true` and a note on the expected format
choices.reason: Correct: input validation errors are tool execution errors, reported in tool results with `isError: true` so models can self-correct and retry.

choices.text: By dropping the request, so the client times out and the model calls it again
choices.reason: A silent drop gives the model nothing to act on; tool execution errors carry actionable feedback models use to self-correct.

choices.text: By removing `book_room` from `tools/list` until a valid date comes in
choices.reason: The tool list MUST NOT vary as a side effect of other requests on the connection; report the bad input in the tool result.

takeaway: MCP: bad **input** to a real tool → result with `isError: true`. Unknown tool or malformed request → protocol error.
explanation: MCP separates **tool execution errors** from **protocol errors**. Bad input to a real tool, such as a wrongly formatted date, is a tool execution error, reported in the result with `isError: true` and a note on the expected format so the model can self-correct and retry (Option B). A is the tempting trap because bad input sounds like a protocol issue, but protocol errors are for unknown tools, malformed requests and server errors, and models recover from them less often. C gives the model nothing to act on, and D changes the tool list, which it must not do.

stem: Your remote MCP server accepts any unexpired access token signed by your company's authorization server, including tokens issued for other internal APIs. According to MCP's authorization guide, what should you fix?

choices.text: Switch the server to stdio so that it never has to accept access tokens
choices.reason: OAuth flows are designed for remotely hosted HTTP servers; stdio servers run locally, so this doesn't secure a server others reach remotely.

choices.text: Log each incoming `Authorization` header so token misuse can be traced later
choices.reason: The guide says never to log `Authorization` headers, tokens, codes or secrets; scrub headers and redact sensitive fields.

choices.text: Issue long-lived tokens so that clients need to re-authorize less often
choices.reason: The guide recommends short-lived access tokens: a stolen long-lived token keeps its access for longer.

choices.text: Check that each token's audience matches your server and reject the rest
choices.reason: Correct: a received token isn't necessarily meant for your server. Require the audience to match your server, which helps avoid token passthrough.

takeaway: Remote MCP server: **always validate tokens**, including the audience, so tokens issued for other APIs are rejected.
explanation: MCP's authorization guide says a token reaching your server isn't necessarily **meant** for it. Accepting any signed, unexpired token lets tokens issued for other internal APIs through, so check that each token's audience matches your server and reject the rest, which also helps avoid token passthrough (Option D). B is the tempting trap because logging seems useful for tracing misuse, but the guide says never to log `Authorization` headers or tokens. A doesn't secure a remote server, and C makes stolen tokens dangerous for longer.

stem: Your Messages API app needs an MCP server's **prompts** and **resources**, not just its tools, and another server it uses runs locally over stdio. Which integration does the MCP connector page point you to?

choices.text: Run your own MCP client and use the SDK's client-side MCP helpers
choices.reason: Correct: use the client-side helpers when you need local servers, prompts, resources, or more control over the connection with the base SDK.

choices.text: Add both servers to `mcp_servers` and list the prompts and resources in each toolset
choices.reason: Of the MCP spec's features, the connector currently supports only tool calls; a toolset configures which tools are enabled.

choices.text: Add the servers to `mcp_servers` with `type: "stdio"` and pass the launch command
choices.reason: `type` currently supports only "url", the URL must start with https://, and local stdio servers can't be connected directly.

choices.text: Pass an `authorization_token` so the connector can fetch the prompts and resources
choices.reason: `authorization_token` is an OAuth token for servers that require one; it doesn't add prompt or resource support to the connector.

takeaway: `mcp_servers` = remote servers, **tools only**. Local servers, prompts or resources → your own MCP client plus the SDK helpers.
explanation: Two needs in the stem rule out the MCP connector: it currently supports only **tool calls**, not prompts or resources, and it can't connect local **stdio** servers. For either case the connector page points to running your own MCP client with the SDK's client-side MCP helpers, which is Option A. C is the tempting trap because it tries to register the stdio server directly, but `type` supports only 'url' with an https URL. B lists features the connector doesn't support, and D's `authorization_token` is only for OAuth.

stem: Claude Code is connected to your Postgres database through an MCP server, and queries run fine. But Claude keeps ignoring your team's table conventions and preferred query patterns. What's the best addition?

choices.text: A second MCP server that exposes the same database with stricter tool descriptions
choices.reason: MCP already provides the connection and tools; knowledge about how to use those tools effectively is what a skill adds.

choices.text: A skill documenting your schema and query patterns, so Claude uses the MCP tools well
choices.reason: Correct: MCP provides the connection and a skill teaches Claude how to use it well, for example your database schema and query patterns.

choices.text: A hook that runs on every prompt and pastes the full schema into the conversation
choices.reason: Hooks suit actions that must run the same way every time without Claude thinking; reference material belongs in a skill that loads on demand.

choices.text: A subagent that owns the database, so the main conversation never runs any queries
choices.reason: Subagents are for context isolation, parallel tasks and specialized workers; the Skill + MCP pattern is the one for teaching query conventions.

takeaway: **MCP** connects; a **skill** teaches. Pair them: the server runs queries, the skill holds the schema and query patterns.
explanation: **MCP connects; a skill teaches.** Queries already run, so the connection works; what's missing is knowledge of your table conventions and query patterns. A skill documenting the schema and query patterns teaches Claude how to use the MCP tools well, which is Option B. A is the tempting trap because better tool descriptions sound like the fix, but MCP already provides the connection and tools, and usage knowledge belongs in a skill. C's hook pastes reference material every time, and D isolates work rather than teaching conventions.

stem: Your team built skills, hooks and an MCP server configuration for one repository. A second repository now needs the exact same setup, and other teams want it too. What fits best?

choices.text: Package them as a plugin and distribute it through a marketplace
choices.reason: Correct: a plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers into one installable unit, to reuse across repositories or distribute via a marketplace.

choices.text: Copy all of it into each repository's CLAUDE.md so it loads at startup
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md holds persistent context Claude sees every session; it doesn't carry hooks or MCP server connections.

choices.text: Move everything into user-level config on each developer's own machine
choices.reason: User-wide definitions belong to one user; the docs' trigger for a second repository needing the same setup is to package it as a plugin.

choices.text: Turn the whole setup into a subagent that every repository can call by name
choices.reason: A subagent is an isolated worker that returns summaries; it doesn't package hooks or MCP servers for other repositories.

takeaway: Same setup needed in a **second repo** or by other teams? Package it as a **plugin**.
explanation: The trigger in the stem is a **second repository** needing the exact same setup, with other teams wanting it too. A plugin bundles skills, hooks, subagents and MCP servers into one installable unit you can reuse across repositories or distribute through a marketplace (Option A). C is the tempting trap because user-level config avoids per-repo copies, but it belongs to one user and doesn't reach other teams. B can't carry hooks or MCP connections, and D's subagent is an isolated worker, not a package.

stem: Your CLAUDE.md has grown to 900 lines, mostly a detailed API reference Claude needs only when working on the payments service. Claude has started missing your core conventions. What does the Claude Code guide recommend?

choices.text: Keep everything in CLAUDE.md, but move the core conventions up to the very top of the file
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md loads in full every session; the guide says to keep it under 200 lines and move reference content to skills.

choices.text: Turn the API reference into an output style so it shapes every response
choices.reason: Output styles set Claude's role, tone and response format for a session; they aren't meant for reference material.

choices.text: Move the API reference into a skill that loads on demand; keep CLAUDE.md lean
choices.reason: Correct: put reference material Claude needs only sometimes in a skill, which loads on demand, and keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines.

choices.text: Put the API reference in a hook that prints it whenever a session starts
choices.reason: Hooks suit actions that must run the same way every time; reference material Claude needs only sometimes belongs in a skill.

takeaway: CLAUDE.md = always-on rules, under 200 lines. Reference material needed only **sometimes** → a skill.
explanation: CLAUDE.md loads **in full every session**, and the guide says to keep it under 200 lines. At 900 lines, mostly payments reference Claude needs only sometimes, it is crowding out the core conventions. Moving the reference into a skill, which loads on demand, keeps CLAUDE.md lean (Option C). A is the tempting trap because reordering seems to fix the missed conventions, but the file still loads in full. B's output styles set role, tone and format, and D's hook is for actions that run every time.

stem: Developers keep copying incident details from a monitoring dashboard in their browser into Claude Code, because Claude can't see that system. Which extension addresses this?

choices.text: A skill describing the dashboard's layout so Claude knows where to look
choices.reason: A skill adds knowledge and workflows; it doesn't give Claude access to an external system's data.

choices.text: An MCP server that connects Claude Code to the monitoring system
choices.reason: Correct: the guide's trigger is exactly this: if you keep copying data from a browser tab Claude can't see, connect that system as an MCP server.

choices.text: A CLAUDE.md section listing the dashboard's URL and its login steps
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md adds context Claude sees every session; it doesn't connect Claude to an external service.

choices.text: A subagent dedicated to reading incident details for the main session
choices.reason: A subagent isolates context and returns summaries; it doesn't connect Claude to an external service on its own.

takeaway: Claude needs data from a system it **can't reach**? Connect that system with **MCP**.
explanation: The guide's trigger is exactly this situation: if you keep copying data from a browser tab Claude **can't see**, connect that system as an MCP server, which is Option B. A is the tempting trap because describing the dashboard seems helpful, but a skill adds knowledge and workflows, not access to an external system's data. C adds context to every session without connecting anything, and D's subagent isolates context but still can't reach the monitoring system on its own.

stem: Your API agent needs to run shell commands in a VM you control. A teammate proposes a custom `run_shell` tool with its own schema instead of Anthropic's `bash` tool. What's the main reason the docs give for preferring the Anthropic-schema tool?

choices.text: Anthropic runs `bash` commands on its own servers, so you don't need to host a VM
choices.reason: `bash` is client-executed: Anthropic publishes the schema, but your application runs each command and returns the result.

choices.text: Custom tools can't run shell commands, because tool inputs must be plain JSON objects only
choices.reason: User-defined tools can call any application logic (a database query, an HTTP call, a file write); the difference is how reliably Claude uses them.

choices.text: Claude is trained on its exact schema, so it calls it more reliably and recovers better
choices.reason: Correct: Anthropic-schema tools are trained-in; Claude has been optimized on thousands of successful trajectories using these exact signatures.

choices.text: The `bash` tool skips the agentic loop, so your code never returns a `tool_result`
choices.reason: The execution model is identical to user-defined tools: a `tool_use` block, your code runs the operation, and you send back a `tool_result`.

takeaway: For shell, file editing, memory or computer use, prefer Anthropic's **trained-in schemas**; your app still executes them.
explanation: Anthropic-schema tools like `bash` are **trained-in**: Claude has been optimized on thousands of successful trajectories using these exact signatures, so it calls them more reliably and recovers better than a custom `run_shell` tool (Option C). A is the tempting trap because Anthropic publishes the `bash` schema, but the tool is client-executed and your application runs each command. B is wrong because custom tools can call any application logic, and D is wrong because the execution model is the same: `tool_use`, your code runs it, `tool_result`.

stem: You want Claude to run Python for ad-hoc data analysis in your API app, but you don't want to host or secure any execution environment yourself. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Anthropic's `bash` tool, since Anthropic publishes and maintains its schema
choices.reason: `bash` is an Anthropic-schema tool, but it's client-executed: your application handles the execution.

choices.text: A custom `run_python` tool whose handler executes the code on your servers
choices.reason: With a user-defined tool you write the schema, execute the code and return the results: the hosting you want to avoid.

choices.text: Anthropic's `text_editor` tool, which writes the scripts and runs them for Claude
choices.reason: `text_editor` is also client-executed: Anthropic publishes the schema and your application performs the operations.

choices.text: The `code_execution` server tool, which Anthropic runs in its own sandbox
choices.reason: Correct: for server-executed tools like `code_execution`, Anthropic runs the code; you enable it and read the results instead of producing them.

takeaway: Need code run with no infrastructure? **`code_execution`** is server-executed; `bash` and `text_editor` run in your app.
explanation: The constraint is **not hosting or securing** any execution environment. `code_execution` is a server-executed tool: Anthropic runs the code in its own sandbox, and you just enable it and read the results (Option D). A is the tempting trap because Anthropic publishes the `bash` schema, but `bash` is client-executed, so your application still runs the commands. C's `text_editor` is client-executed too, and B's custom tool means writing the schema and executing the code yourself.

stem: A teammate found a handy community Skill from an unknown author for processing invoices and wants to add it to your production agent, which can access customer data. What does Anthropic's Skills guidance say to do?

choices.text: Read the SKILL.md description; if it matches the stated purpose, the Skill is safe
choices.reason: A malicious Skill can direct Claude to act in ways that don't match its stated purpose; review SKILL.md, scripts, images and other resources.

choices.text: Audit every bundled file, scripts included, as you would before installing software
choices.reason: Correct: use Skills only from trusted sources; if you must use an unknown one, audit it thoroughly and treat it like installing software.

choices.text: Install it, because Skills only add instructions and can't execute any code
choices.reason: Skills bundle executable scripts, and malicious Skills can invoke tools such as bash commands or code execution in harmful ways.

choices.text: Install it, since every Skill runs in a sandbox that blocks all outgoing network calls
choices.reason: Network access depends on the surface (Claude Code Skills have full network access), and Skills with data access could leak it externally.

takeaway: Treat a Skill like **software**: trusted sources only, and audit every file, scripts included, before production use.
explanation: Treat a Skill like **installing software**. Skills bundle executable scripts and can invoke tools such as bash or code execution, so a Skill from an unknown author must be audited thoroughly, every file included, before it touches customer data (Option B). A is the tempting trap: a matching description proves nothing, because a malicious Skill can act differently from its stated purpose. C wrongly says Skills can't run code, and D wrongly assumes a sandbox, since Claude Code Skills have full network access.

stem: You're moving your team's practices into Claude Code extensions. Which of these belong in hooks rather than skills?

choices.text: Blocking any edit to `.env` files, with no exceptions
choices.reason: Correct: a rule that must hold every time belongs in a hook; a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks the edit is enforcement, not a request.

choices.text: A `/release` checklist that Claude adapts to each release
choices.reason: A checklist Claude decides how to apply is the docs' own example of a skill: a `/release` checklist.

choices.text: Your API style guide, for Claude to consult while coding
choices.reason: Reference material such as an API style guide is knowledge rather than a script, so it belongs in a skill.

choices.text: A debugging playbook Claude applies to each new bug
choices.reason: A debugging playbook needs Claude to decide how to apply the steps, which makes it a skill, not a hook.

choices.text: Posting a Slack message whenever a session ends
choices.reason: Correct: an action that should happen the same way every time without Claude thinking, like posting to Slack when a session ends, is a hook.

takeaway: **Hook** = fires every time, no judgment (block, lint, notify). **Skill** = knowledge or steps Claude applies with judgment.
explanation: The dividing line is **judgment**. A hook fires every time with no thinking, so it fits a rule that must always hold, like blocking any edit to `.env` (A), and a fixed action like posting to Slack when a session ends (E). B is the most tempting wrong pick because a release checklist sounds procedural, but Claude adapts it to each release, and the docs use `/release` as a skill example. The style guide (C) is reference knowledge, and the debugging playbook (D) needs Claude to decide how to apply it, so both are skills.

stem: Your invoice Skill describes how to validate a form, and Claude writes fresh validation code from those instructions on every run. Results vary and token use is high. What does the Agent Skills overview suggest?

choices.text: Paste the full validation code into SKILL.md so Claude can copy it on every run
choices.reason: The SKILL.md body enters context when the Skill triggers; a bundled script's code never does, and running it is more reliable.

choices.text: Move the validation steps into the Skill's `description` so they're always in context
choices.reason: The description is Level 1 metadata (~100 tokens per Skill) that Claude matches to decide when to trigger; it isn't where procedures go.

choices.text: Bundle a `validate.py` script that Claude runs, so only its output enters context
choices.reason: Correct: scripts give deterministic operations, and only their output uses tokens, making them far more efficient than generating equivalent code.

choices.text: Split the steps into several smaller Skills, each with its own trigger description
choices.reason: More Skills still leave Claude generating the code each time; bundled scripts are how a Skill gets reliable, low-token operations.

takeaway: Deterministic step in a Skill? Ship it as a **script**: Claude runs it, and only the output costs tokens.
explanation: When a Skill step is **deterministic**, ship it as a script. A bundled `validate.py` that Claude runs gives consistent results, and only its output uses tokens, which is far more efficient than generating equivalent code each run (Option C). A is the tempting trap because pasted code seems reusable, but the SKILL.md body enters context when the Skill triggers, while a bundled script's code never does. B misuses the description, which is trigger metadata, and D still leaves Claude generating code every time.

stem: Claude's response to your app contains a `text` block followed by a `tool_use` block with `id: "toolu_01A"` for your `lookup_order` tool. Which statements about these blocks and your reply are correct?

choices.text: Claude produced both the `text` and the `tool_use` block; both belong to the assistant message
choices.reason: Correct: assistant messages contain AI-generated content and `tool_use`; the docs' example shows Claude's `text` block before its `tool_use`.

choices.text: Your `tool_result` goes in an assistant message placed right after the `tool_use` block
choices.reason: Results go in a **user** message: user messages carry client content and `tool_result`, assistant messages carry `tool_use`.

choices.text: Your reply may open with a text block explaining the result, as long as the `tool_result` follows it
choices.reason: Text before a `tool_result` causes a 400 error: tool_result blocks must come first, and any text comes after them.

choices.text: Your `tool_result` carries `tool_use_id: "toolu_01A"` and goes in the next user message
choices.reason: Correct: `tool_use_id` matches the result to its call, and the result goes in a user message right after the assistant turn.

choices.text: The order lookup runs on Anthropic's side, and its output arrives as a `tool_result` in Claude's next response
choices.reason: `lookup_order` is a client tool: you extract the input, run the tool in your codebase and send the result yourself.

takeaway: Claude writes `text` and `tool_use` in the assistant turn; you answer with `tool_result` blocks, first, in the next user message.
explanation: The Claude API has no special tool role: tools live inside ordinary user and assistant messages. Claude produced both blocks in its response, and your reply is a user message whose `tool_result` echoes `toolu_01A`. Choice c is the tempting one, since a lead-in sentence seems harmless, but text before a `tool_result` returns a 400 error.

stem: Your agent runs with thinking on. A response contains a `thinking` block and a `tool_use` block. To save input tokens, your code sends back only the `tool_use` block in the assistant message, plus the `tool_result`. What does Anthropic's thinking guide say to do?

choices.text: Keep dropping it: thinking only affects the first response, and the tool result has what Claude needs
choices.reason: Claude continues building the **same** response after the result, so the reasoning that led to the call must still be present.

choices.text: Copy the thinking text into the `tool_result` content so Claude sees its reasoning next to the result
choices.reason: Thinking blocks go back in the assistant message next to their `tool_use` block. They can't be rearranged or edited.

choices.text: Pass the `thinking` block back complete and unmodified, alongside the `tool_use` block it came with
choices.reason: Correct: within a tool-use turn, passing thinking blocks back unchanged is required, for reasoning continuity and context.

choices.text: Turn thinking off for the follow-up request, so the missing block no longer matters
choices.reason: A tool-use loop is one assistant turn in one thinking mode. Toggling mid-turn silently disables thinking for that request.

takeaway: Within a tool-use turn, `thinking` blocks go back to the API unchanged, next to their `tool_use` blocks.
explanation: When Claude calls a tool it pauses its response, and your `tool_result` lets it resume that same response, so its earlier reasoning must travel with it. The detail that decides it is that the blocks are dropped inside an unfinished tool-use turn. Choice d looks like a clean workaround, but switching thinking mid-turn just silently disables thinking for that request.

stem: Your `get_order_total` tool's code converts every amount to EUR, but its description doesn't say so. Claude keeps telling customers their totals are in USD. Where did Claude's knowledge of this tool come from?

choices.text: From the tool's source code, which the API reads when it builds the tool-use system prompt
choices.reason: The page says Claude never sees your implementation, so the source code is not where its picture of the tool came from.

choices.text: From the `tool_use` block, which carries the currency the tool will return
choices.reason: A `tool_use` block carries the tool name and a JSON object of arguments. It says nothing about what the tool returns.

choices.text: From earlier customer conversations, which teach Claude the tool's behavior over time
choices.reason: Per the page, Claude sees only the schema you provided and the result you returned; past traffic isn't part of that.

choices.text: Only from the schema you wrote and the results you send back in `tool_result` blocks
choices.reason: Correct: Claude never sees your implementation, only the schema you provided and the result you returned.

takeaway: Claude knows a tool only through its schema and its results, so a behavior they don't mention is invisible to it.
explanation: Tool use is a contract: Claude sees the schema you provided and the results you returned, never the code. Here the EUR conversion appears in neither: the description is silent and the results evidently don't make it clear. Choice a is the tempting misconception, but Claude never sees your implementation. Say what the tool returns in its description.

stem: Claude asked for `get_weather` and your code has the result: "15 degrees". What should the next request to the Messages API contain?

choices.text: The original messages, Claude's assistant response, and a user message holding the `tool_result`
choices.reason: Correct: step 4 of the loop sends the original messages, the assistant's response, and a user message with the `tool_result` blocks.

choices.text: Only a user message with the `tool_result`, since the API keeps the rest of the conversation for you
choices.reason: Each request carries the conversation: the loop's new request includes the original messages and the assistant's response.

choices.text: The original messages, with "15 degrees" appended to the system prompt as tool output
choices.reason: Step 4 puts results in `tool_result` blocks inside a user message, not in the system prompt.

choices.text: An assistant message holding the result, so Claude continues as if it had produced the answer
choices.reason: The result is your application's report, sent as a `tool_result` in a **user** message, not an assistant message.

takeaway: After running a tool, resend the whole conversation: the original messages, Claude's response, then a user message with the `tool_result`.
explanation: The loop's fourth step resends the conversation, now including Claude's `tool_use` turn and your answer to it. The deciding detail is that the API needs both the call and its result in history. Choice b is tempting because it seems efficient, but a new request containing only the result loses the original question and the call it answers.

diagram.caption: Step 4 of the loop: what the next request carries.

stem: Your agent spans GitHub and Slack. It has tools `list_items` (description: "Lists items.") and `search` (description: "Searches."), one for each service. Claude often calls the Slack tool for GitHub questions. Which changes does Anthropic's Define tools guide recommend?

choices.text: Set `strict: true` on both tools so Claude's calls follow the schema exactly
choices.reason: Strict tool use guarantees inputs match the schema; it doesn't help Claude choose between two tools.

choices.text: Prefix each tool's name with its service, such as `github_list_prs` and `slack_send_message`
choices.reason: Correct: namespacing by service makes tool selection unambiguous as your tool library grows.

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to `any` so Claude must pick one of the tools on every turn
choices.reason: `any` forces some tool call but not the right one, and some current models reject it with a 400 error.

choices.text: Rewrite each description: what the tool does, when to use it and when not, and what each parameter means
choices.reason: Correct: detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor in tool performance.

choices.text: Cut each description to a few words so the tool definitions cost fewer input tokens
choices.reason: The guide asks for at least 3–4 sentences per description; cutting them makes selection worse.

takeaway: When Claude mixes up tools, fix the schema: detailed descriptions first, then service-prefixed names.
explanation: Claude chooses tools from their names and descriptions, and here both are too vague to tell the services apart. Rich descriptions are the biggest lever, and service prefixes make the choice unambiguous. Choice a is tempting because strict mode sounds like tighter control, but it governs inputs, not which tool gets picked.

stem: Your `get_account` tool takes a parameter named `user`, and the code expects a numeric account ID. Claude keeps passing a person's name or email address instead. What does Anthropic's post on writing tools for agents suggest?

choices.text: Name the parameter unambiguously, such as `user_id` instead of `user`
choices.reason: Correct: the post says inputs should be unambiguously named, for example `user_id` rather than `user`.

choices.text: Leave the name and have your code try the value as an ID, then a name, then an email
choices.reason: That hides the ambiguity instead of removing it. The post fixes it in the tool spec, which Claude reads.

choices.text: Split it into `get_account_by_id`, `get_account_by_name` and `get_account_by_email` tools
choices.reason: The post warns that more tools and overlapping tools can distract agents. The problem is the vague name.

choices.text: Shorten the description so Claude focuses on the parameter list rather than the prose
choices.reason: The post says descriptions and specs should make implicit context explicit, as you would for a new hire.

takeaway: A parameter name is part of the spec Claude reads: `user_id` says what `user` only implies.
explanation: Claude fills inputs from what the tool spec tells it, and `user` could mean a name, an email or an ID. Renaming it `user_id` makes the expected value explicit. Choice c is tempting because each tool would be narrower, but it adds overlapping tools, which the post warns can distract agents.

stem: Your agent books meetings with three tools: `list_users`, `list_events` and `create_event`. Every booking chains all three, and the agent burns context on intermediate output. What does Anthropic's post on writing tools for agents suggest?

choices.text: Add a fourth tool, `check_availability`, so each step of the chain is smaller and easier to call
choices.reason: More tools don't always lead to better outcomes, and too many or overlapping tools can distract agents.

choices.text: Replace them with a `schedule_event` tool that finds availability and schedules the event
choices.reason: Correct: the post suggests exactly this, consolidating frequently chained, multi-step tasks into a single tool call.

choices.text: Return the full output of every call, so Claude has complete data for the next step
choices.reason: The post says agents' context is limited and recommends tools that return only relevant information.

choices.text: Keep the tools, but have each one wrap its API endpoint exactly as it is
choices.reason: The post names tools that merely wrap existing API endpoints as a common error, since agents have different affordances.

takeaway: Steps that always run together can be one tool: build for the workflow (`schedule_event`), not for each API endpoint.
explanation: When subtasks always depend on each other, splitting them across tools costs round trips and the context of intermediate outputs. The post's own example replaces `list_users`, `list_events` and `create_event` with `schedule_event`. Choice a is tempting because smaller steps feel simpler, but it adds tools and makes the chain longer.

stem: In code review, a teammate asks you to cut every tool description to one short line, because the `tools` array counts toward input tokens. What does Anthropic's Define tools guide recommend?

choices.text: One line per tool, with the detail moved into `input_examples` instead
choices.reason: Descriptions are what matter most; `input_examples` is an extra for complex inputs, not a replacement for them.

choices.text: One line per tool; Claude picks tools from their names, so long descriptions add cost without effect
choices.reason: The guide calls detailed descriptions by far the most important factor in tool performance.

choices.text: Move the tool details into the system prompt and keep each description to a few words
choices.reason: The guide asks for the detail in each tool's description: what it does, when to use it, parameters and caveats.

choices.text: Aim for at least 3–4 sentences per description, more if the tool is complex
choices.reason: Correct: the guide sets this target, because detailed descriptions are by far the most important factor.

takeaway: Tool descriptions are the biggest lever on tool performance: aim for 3–4+ sentences each.
explanation: Tool definitions do cost input tokens, but the guide ranks detailed descriptions as by far the most important factor in how well Claude uses tools. The decisive detail is that the trade-off goes against brevity. Choice a sounds like a compromise, but examples supplement descriptions for complex inputs; they don't replace them.

stem: Your AI application runs its own MCP client connected to a weather MCP server. You passed the server's tools to the model, and the model now calls `weather_current`. According to the MCP architecture docs, what happens next?

choices.text: The model connects to the MCP server itself and runs `weather_current` directly
choices.reason: The model only emits the call. The application intercepts it and does the routing and execution.

choices.text: Your app routes the call to that server with `tools/call` and returns the result to the model
choices.reason: Correct: the application intercepts the tool call, routes it to the right MCP server, and returns the result to the model.

choices.text: The server pushes the result into the model's context with a `notifications/tools/list_changed` message
choices.reason: That notification signals that the server's tool list changed. Tool results come back as the response to `tools/call`.

choices.text: Your app first re-sends `tools/list`, because the model can only call tools listed in the same request
choices.reason: Discovery already happened; tools are listed up front. Executing a discovered tool uses `tools/call`.

takeaway: MCP keeps the loop: your app routes each tool call to its server with `tools/call` and hands the result back to the model.
explanation: MCP changes who writes and runs the tools, not the loop. The app discovered the tools with `tools/list`; when the model calls one, the app routes it to the owning server with `tools/call` and adds the result to the conversation. Choice a is tempting because the tool lives on the server, but the model never executes anything itself.

stem: Instead of hand-writing tool schemas for a vendor's API, your application connects to the vendor's MCP server. Which parts of the tool work does the server now supply?

choices.text: Each tool's `name`, `description` and `inputSchema`, returned by `tools/list`
choices.reason: Correct: each tool object from `tools/list` has a name, a description of what it does and when to use it, and an `inputSchema`.

choices.text: The choice of which tool to call for each user request
choices.reason: The language model decides when to use a tool; the server only lists and runs tools.

choices.text: Routing each tool call to the right server and adding the result to the conversation
choices.reason: That's the AI application's job: it intercepts the call, routes it to the right server and returns the result to the model.

choices.text: Running the tool's logic when it receives a `tools/call` request
choices.reason: Correct: the client invokes a discovered tool with `tools/call`, and the server executes it and returns the content.

choices.text: Tool-change notifications to every client, whether or not it subscribed
choices.reason: Change notifications are opt-in: a client gets them only after asking with `subscriptions/listen`.

takeaway: An MCP server supplies the tool schemas (`tools/list`) and runs the calls (`tools/call`); the app and the model keep their roles.
explanation: With MCP, the server takes over what you'd otherwise write yourself: the schema (name, description, `inputSchema`) and the implementation. The model still decides which tool to call, and the application still routes calls and feeds results back. Choice c is tempting because the server seems to handle everything, but routing and returning results are the host application's job.

stem: Your Messages API app needs Claude to use your company's proprietary pricing engine, a function in your own backend. No MCP server exists for it and no other app needs it. Which approach does Anthropic's How tool use works page fit to this case?

choices.text: Write a user-defined tool: your own name, description and `input_schema`, run by your code
choices.reason: Correct: user-defined client tools fit custom business logic, internal APIs and proprietary data; you write the schema and run the code.

choices.text: Enable a server tool such as `code_execution` so Anthropic runs the pricing logic
choices.reason: Server tools such as `code_execution` run on Anthropic's infrastructure; your pricing function lives in your own backend.

choices.text: Describe the pricing rules in the system prompt, then parse the final price out of Claude's text reply
choices.reason: The page warns that if you're writing a regex to pull a decision out of model output, that decision should have been a tool call.

choices.text: Use Anthropic's `bash` tool, which Claude calls more reliably than any tool you define
choices.reason: Anthropic-schema tools fit standard operations like shell commands, not your application's own business logic.

takeaway: Custom business logic, internal APIs and proprietary data are the job of user-defined tools you write and run yourself.
explanation: Writing schemas yourself is the right call when the tool is your own logic and no one else has built it. Here the pricing engine is proprietary, lives in your backend and has no MCP server. Choice d is tempting because the page says trained-in schemas are called more reliably, but that applies to standard operations such as shell commands, not your pricing logic.

stem: Your team owns an MCP server whose `find` tool is described only as "Finds things." Connected through the MCP connector next to other servers, Claude often uses another server's tool for questions `find` should answer. A teammate says descriptions don't matter for MCP tools. What's right?

choices.text: Your teammate is right: the MCP server, not Claude, chooses which tool handles each request
choices.reason: Claude calls an MCP tool when the user's request maps to the tool's described capability; the server doesn't choose.

choices.text: Add your own description for `find` in the `mcp_servers` entry, which overrides the server's version
choices.reason: An `mcp_servers` entry holds connection details such as the URL and authorization, not tool descriptions.

choices.text: Set `defer_loading: true` on `find` so Claude reads its description only when it's needed
choices.reason: Deferred loading keeps a description out of the initial context; it doesn't make a vague description clearer.

choices.text: Claude picks MCP tools by name and description too, so rewrite `find`'s description on your server
choices.reason: Correct: with many tools, Claude selects based on names and descriptions, and clear, specific descriptions improve accuracy.

takeaway: MCP tool descriptions steer Claude's choice just like your own; if you own the server, fix them there.
explanation: An MCP server's tools reach Claude as names and descriptions, and Claude selects among them exactly as it does for tools you define. The connector page notes that clear, specific descriptions improve selection accuracy. Choice c is tempting because it's a connector setting, but deferred loading decides when a description is loaded, not whether it's any good.

stem: Your loop is written as `while stop_reason != "end_turn"`: run the tools, send the results, repeat. One response comes back with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` and no `tool_use` block, and the loop keeps resending the conversation. What should the loop condition be?

choices.text: Keep the condition but cap the loop at a fixed number of iterations, so it always stops eventually
choices.reason: A cap only limits the damage. The loop should continue only while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`; `max_tokens` is a stop your app should handle.

choices.text: Loop while `stop_reason` is `"end_turn"` or `"tool_use"`, so both cases reach your tool-running code
choices.reason: `end_turn` means Claude has produced a final answer. It is an exit condition, not a reason to run tools again.

choices.text: Loop only while `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, and handle every other stop reason after exiting
choices.reason: Correct: the canonical loop is keyed on `stop_reason == "tool_use"` and exits on `end_turn`, `max_tokens`, `stop_sequence` or `refusal`.

choices.text: Loop while the response contains a `text` block, since text means Claude still has more to say
choices.reason: The loop is keyed on `stop_reason`, not on block types; a final answer is text too, so this test would never exit.

takeaway: Continue only on `stop_reason: "tool_use"`; any other stop reason ends the loop for your app to handle.
explanation: The tool-use loop is a while loop keyed on one value: `tool_use` means run the tools and continue, and anything else exits. The deciding detail is the `max_tokens` response with no tool call, which a `!= "end_turn"` test wrongly treats as more tool work. Choice a is tempting as a safety net, but a cap only limits the damage; the condition itself is wrong.

stem: You're porting an agent from an API that sends tool output in a message with a dedicated `tool` role. On the Claude API, how should your code send back the output of Claude's `get_weather` call?

choices.text: In a `system` message added after Claude's response, holding the raw tool output
choices.reason: Tool output goes in `tool_result` blocks inside a `user` message, not in a system message.
