choices.text: In an `assistant` message, since the output continues Claude's own turn
choices.reason: `assistant` messages hold AI-generated content and `tool_use`; client content and `tool_result` go in `user` messages.

choices.text: In a message with the `function` role, which the Claude API uses in place of the `tool` role
choices.reason: Unlike APIs with special `tool` or `function` roles, the Claude API builds tools into the `user` and `assistant` messages.

choices.text: As a `tool_result` block carrying the call's `tool_use_id`, in the next `user` message
choices.reason: Correct: `user` messages carry client content and `tool_result` blocks, and each result names its call with `tool_use_id`.

takeaway: The Claude API has no `tool` role: results travel as `tool_result` blocks in a `user` message.
explanation: The Claude API keeps tool traffic inside the ordinary roles: Claude's calls are `tool_use` blocks in the assistant message, and your outputs are `tool_result` blocks in the next user message. The deciding detail is the ported `tool` role, which this API doesn't have. Choice c is tempting because some APIs use a `function` role, but the Claude API uses neither special role.

stem: Your `book_flight` tool hits a rate limit, and your code returns a `tool_result` with `"is_error": true` and the content `"failed"`. Claude tells the user the booking is impossible instead of suggesting a retry. What does Anthropic's Handle tool calls page suggest?

choices.text: Say what went wrong and what to try next, such as "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds."
choices.reason: Correct: instead of generic errors like "failed", include what went wrong and what Claude should try next, so it can recover or adapt without guessing.

choices.text: Drop `is_error` and send an empty `tool_result`, so Claude doesn't treat the call as a failure at all
choices.reason: That hides the failure. For a tool execution error, the page says to return the message in `content` with `"is_error": true`.

choices.text: Skip the `tool_result` for this call and send a plain user text message that explains the rate limit instead
choices.reason: Each `tool_use` needs its `tool_result` immediately after it; the error message belongs in that result's `content`.

choices.text: Return an HTTP error from your server so the Messages API retries the tool call on its own
choices.reason: The API doesn't run client tools. Your code reports the failure in a `tool_result`, and Claude incorporates the error into its response.

takeaway: Tool errors should teach: say what failed and what Claude should try next, not just "failed".
explanation: An `is_error` result lets Claude recover only if its content says how. The deciding detail is the bare "failed": Claude can't tell a temporary rate limit from a permanent failure, so it gives up. Choice b is tempting because it avoids the error path, but it hides the very failure the page says to report with `is_error: true`.

stem: Claude's responses often open with a `text` block such as "I'll check the weather for you." before a `tool_use` block. Your dispatcher matches that sentence with a regex to decide which tool to run, and it breaks whenever the wording changes. Which two statements match Anthropic's Define tools guide?

choices.text: Pin the wording with a template in the system prompt, then keep the regex as the dispatcher
choices.reason: Claude may use various phrasings when explaining its actions, so your code shouldn't rely on formatting in that text.

choices.text: Treat that text like any other assistant-generated text, without relying on its exact wording
choices.reason: Correct: the guide says to treat these responses like any other assistant text and not rely on specific formatting conventions.

choices.text: Every `tool_use` block comes after a `text` block, so the text is a reliable delimiter for calls
choices.reason: Claude often comments first, not always: with `tool_choice` `any` or `tool`, no natural-language text comes before `tool_use`.

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` to `any` so that Claude explains each call in more detail before making it
choices.reason: The reverse: with `any` or `tool`, the API prefills the turn and Claude won't write an explanation before `tool_use`, even if asked.

choices.text: Dispatch on the `tool_use` block: its `name` picks the tool and its `input` holds the arguments
choices.reason: Correct: a `tool_use` block carries the tool `name` and an `input` object, as in the guide's example response.

takeaway: Run tools from the `tool_use` block's `name` and `input`; treat the text before it as ordinary prose.
explanation: The structured call lives in the `tool_use` block, while the text before it is commentary whose wording varies. The deciding detail is a regex that breaks when the wording changes: the guide says not to rely on that text's formatting. Choice c is tempting because the comment usually appears, but forced tool use removes it entirely, so it can't serve as a delimiter.

stem: When Claude calls a tool, your app appends two user messages: one with the text "Reminder: keep answers short", then one with the `tool_result`. The API returns an error saying tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after. What fixes it?

choices.text: Send one user message right after Claude's turn: the `tool_result` first, the reminder after it
choices.reason: Correct: tool results must immediately follow their tool use blocks with no messages in between, and text may come after all results.

choices.text: Merge the two into one user message, with the reminder text first and the `tool_result` after it
choices.reason: In the user message holding tool results, `tool_result` blocks must come first; text before them causes a 400 error.

choices.text: Send the `tool_result` in an assistant message instead, so nothing can separate it from the call
choices.reason: `assistant` messages hold AI-generated content and `tool_use`; `tool_result` blocks go in a `user` message.

choices.text: Add `"is_error": true` to the `tool_result` so the API accepts it after the other user message
choices.reason: `is_error` marks a failed tool execution. It doesn't relax the rule that results immediately follow their tool use blocks.

takeaway: Nothing may sit between a `tool_use` turn and its results; extra text goes after the results in the same user message.
explanation: The API expects each `tool_use` to be answered by a `tool_result` in the very next message. The deciding detail is the separate reminder message wedged between the call and its result. Choice b is tempting because it removes the extra message, but placing text before the `tool_result` in that message is its own 400 error.

stem: A security reviewer looks at your plan to give Claude a user-defined `issue_refund` tool. They worry that once the tool is defined, Claude can issue refunds on its own. What does Anthropic's description of the tool-use contract say?

choices.text: Claude runs the tool's code inside the API once its schema is valid, so the definition is the only control
choices.reason: The model never executes anything on its own. For user-defined tools, your application runs the operation.

choices.text: Anthropic's servers run every tool you define and return its result in the same response
choices.reason: Only server tools such as `web_search` and `code_execution` run on Anthropic's side; you execute the tools you define.

choices.text: Claude only emits a structured `tool_use` request; your application's code is what runs the refund
choices.reason: Correct: Claude emits a structured request, your code runs the operation, and the result flows back into the conversation.

choices.text: Claude calls your refund API directly, using the arguments described in `input_schema`
choices.reason: Claude never sees your implementation; it only sees the schema you provided and the result you returned.

takeaway: Claude asks, your code acts: a user-defined tool runs only when your application executes the `tool_use` request.
explanation: Tool use is a contract: Claude decides when to call a tool and with what input, but the model never executes anything itself. The deciding detail is that `issue_refund` is user-defined, so it runs in your code, where you control it. Choice b is tempting because some tools do run on Anthropic's servers, but that applies only to server tools such as `web_search`.

stem: Claude calls your `archive_thread` tool. It succeeds but produces no output, so a teammate's code sends nothing back for that call. What should the next user message contain?

choices.text: A text block saying "done", since a `tool_result` is only needed when a tool returns data
choices.reason: Every client tool call is answered with a `tool_result`; the page even shows a valid result with no content.

choices.text: A `tool_result` with the call's `tool_use_id`, leaving out the optional `content` field
choices.reason: Correct: `content` is optional. The page's empty-result example has only the type and `tool_use_id`.

choices.text: A `tool_result` with `"is_error": true`, because a call with no output counts as a failure
choices.reason: `is_error` is for when the tool execution resulted in an error; a successful call with no output is not one.

choices.text: Nothing: Claude continues once the next request includes its own `tool_use` turn again
choices.reason: A `tool_use` must be followed by its `tool_result`; otherwise the API reports tool_use ids found without tool_result blocks.

takeaway: Every client tool call gets a `tool_result`, even an empty one: `content` is optional, `tool_use_id` is not.
explanation: Each `tool_use` block must be answered by a `tool_result` that names it with `tool_use_id`, whether or not the tool produced output. The deciding detail is that the call succeeded, so the result simply has no content. Choice c is tempting because an empty output feels like a problem, but `is_error` is for failed executions, not silent successes.

stem: Your `read_inbox` tool returns the bodies of emails from outside senders. A teammate wants to move each body out of the `tool_result` and into a plain `text` block after the results, so Claude treats the email as part of the user's request. What does Anthropic's Handle tool calls page advise?

choices.text: Move them: text is allowed after the results, so each email reads as part of the user's request
choices.reason: Text may follow the results, but the page lists plain user `text` blocks among the places to keep untrusted content out of.

choices.text: Move them into the `system` prompt instead, so Claude reads each email more carefully
choices.reason: The page says to keep untrusted content inside `tool_result` blocks rather than in `system` prompts.

choices.text: Put each body into the `tool_use` block's `input`, so the content stays attached to the call
choices.reason: `tool_use` blocks are Claude's calls in the assistant message; your app returns tool output in `tool_result` blocks.

choices.text: Keep them in `tool_result` blocks, since outside content is untrusted and may carry prompt injection
choices.reason: Correct: an attacker who influences that content may embed instructions (indirect prompt injection), so keep it inside `tool_result` blocks.

takeaway: Keep content from outside sources inside `tool_result` blocks, not in `system` prompts or plain user `text` blocks.
explanation: Tool results often carry content you don't control, such as inbound email, and an attacker who can influence it may embed instructions meant to redirect Claude. The deciding detail is the move into a plain user `text` block, which presents an outsider's words as the user's own request. Choice a is tempting because text after the results is valid formatting, but valid formatting isn't the same as safe placement for untrusted content.

stem: A teammate copies every tool's description into your system prompt as well as the `tools` array, "so Claude can see the tools". What does Anthropic's Define tools guide say happens when you send `tools`?

choices.text: The API builds a special system prompt from the tool definitions, so Claude already sees them
choices.reason: Correct: with `tools`, the API constructs a special system prompt from the tool definitions, tool configuration and your system prompt.

choices.text: The definitions only validate Claude's calls, so they must be repeated in the system prompt
choices.reason: The constructed system prompt includes the tool definitions in JSON Schema format, so Claude does see them.

choices.text: Claude reads only the tool names from `tools`; the descriptions reach the model only through the system prompt
choices.reason: The constructed prompt carries the full tool definitions in JSON Schema, descriptions included.

choices.text: The `tools` array replaces your own system prompt, so all of your guidance has to move into the descriptions
choices.reason: The constructed prompt keeps your system prompt: its template includes the user system prompt next to the tool definitions.

takeaway: Sending `tools` already puts your definitions in front of Claude, inside a system prompt the API builds for you.
explanation: When a request includes `tools`, the API assembles a tool-use system prompt containing the definitions, the tool configuration and your own system prompt. The deciding detail is the teammate's belief that Claude can't see the `tools` array. Choice d is tempting because the API does build a new prompt, but your system prompt is kept inside it, not replaced.

stem: In one response, Claude returns three `tool_use` blocks: `get_invoice` and `get_customer`, which only read data, and `send_reminder`, which emails the customer. You decide how to run them. Which two choices fit Anthropic's Parallel tool use guide?

choices.text: Run the two read-only lookups concurrently; independent reads are usually safe in parallel
choices.reason: Correct: independent, read-only operations are usually safe to run in parallel for lower latency.

choices.text: Run all three strictly in the order they appear, because the API requires sequential execution
choices.reason: The API doesn't prescribe an order: you can run calls concurrently, sequentially or in any combination.

choices.text: Send each tool's result in its own user message as soon as that particular tool finishes
choices.reason: Return every `tool_result` together in the next user message; separate messages teach Claude to avoid parallel calls.

choices.text: Consider running `send_reminder` separately: side-effect calls may be better sequential
choices.reason: Correct: tools with side effects, shared state or ordering requirements might be better run sequentially.

choices.text: Put a short text block before the three results that says which calls ran in parallel
choices.reason: Every `tool_result` block must come before any text content in that user message.

takeaway: You choose how a batch runs: parallel for independent reads, sequential for side effects; results always return together.
explanation: Claude can request several tools at once, but execution strategy is yours, based on what each tool does. The deciding detail is the mix: two harmless reads and one call that sends an email. Choice b is tempting because order feels safer, but the API prescribes no execution order; the guide ties the choice to side effects and dependencies.

stem: Your `get_weather` tool needs a `location` on every call, while `unit` (celsius or fahrenheit) is optional. How should its `input_schema` express this?

choices.text: List both fields in `required`, and say in the description of `unit` that it can be left empty
choices.reason: Fields in `required` must be supplied. An optional field is defined in `properties` but left out of `required`.

choices.text: Define only `location` in `properties` and mention `unit` in the tool description instead
choices.reason: Then `unit` has no type or allowed values; the guide's example defines it in `properties` with an `enum`.

choices.text: Define both in `properties`, list only `location` in `required`, and give `unit` an `enum`
choices.reason: Correct: this is the guide's own example, a required `location` string and an optional `unit` limited to "celsius" or "fahrenheit".

choices.text: Create two separate tools, `get_weather_c` and `get_weather_f`, so neither one needs an optional field
choices.reason: The guide favors fewer, more capable tools; near-duplicate tools add selection ambiguity.

takeaway: Optional means defined in `properties` but left out of `required`; an `enum` pins down its allowed values.
explanation: Required and optional fields are both declared in `properties`; the `required` array is what separates them. The deciding detail is that `unit` has a fixed set of values, which an `enum` captures. Choice a is tempting because the description seems to explain the field is optional, but listing it in `required` tells Claude it must always be supplied.

stem: Claude sometimes requests `create_order` and `charge_order` in the same response, even though `charge_order` needs the order ID that `create_order` returns. Run in parallel, the charge fails. What does the Parallel tool use guide suggest to reduce dependent calls appearing together?

choices.text: Add "Only batch tool calls that are independent of each other." to your system prompt
choices.reason: Correct: the guide suggests exactly this system-prompt line to reduce dependent calls appearing together.

choices.text: Set `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` as a top-level parameter of the request
choices.reason: It isn't a top-level request parameter; it goes inside the `tool_choice` object, and it limits every call, not just dependent ones.

choices.text: Return the two results in separate user messages so Claude learns the calls belong to different steps
choices.reason: Separate messages per result is the most common formatting mistake, and it teaches Claude to avoid parallel calls in general.

choices.text: Keep running the batch in parallel, and leave out the `tool_result` for the charge that failed
choices.reason: Return `is_error: true` with the natural error message for the failed call; Claude will reissue it on the next turn.

takeaway: To keep dependent calls out of one batch, say so in the system prompt: only batch calls that are independent.
explanation: Claude may batch calls that look independent but aren't, and the guide's targeted fix is a system-prompt instruction. The deciding detail is that the goal is fewer dependent calls together, not fewer parallel calls overall. Choice b is tempting because it stops batching, but it isn't a top-level parameter and it would also block the independent calls you want in parallel.

diagram.caption: `charge_order` depends on the output of `create_order`.

stem: Your `search_news` tool works, but Claude keeps adding the current year to every query, which skews results toward that year's articles. You own the tool. Based on Anthropic's post on writing tools for agents, what should you try first?

choices.text: Strip the year from each query in code before the search runs
choices.reason: The post fixed this same habit by improving the tool description, steering Claude instead of patching its queries afterwards.

choices.text: Improve the tool description to steer how Claude writes its queries
choices.reason: Correct: the post saw Claude needlessly appending the year to search queries and fixed it by improving the tool description.

choices.text: Split the tool into one search tool per year so Claude picks a range
choices.reason: The post's fix for this habit was a better description, not more tools for Claude to choose between.

choices.text: Move to a larger model, since query habits like this come from size
choices.reason: The post didn't treat it as a model-size problem; improving the description alone steered Claude the right way.

takeaway: When Claude misuses a tool parameter, **improve the tool description** first: Anthropic fixed this exact habit that way.
explanation: Tool descriptions act as prompts, so a bad parameter habit is often a description problem. Anthropic saw Claude needlessly appending the year to web search queries and steered it **by improving the tool description** (B). A is the tempting trap because it works mechanically, but it would also strip years that users really asked for. C and D add tools or cost without addressing the cause.

source.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents

stem: With the default `tool_choice`, Claude calls your `get_exchange_rate` tool for "What's today's EUR to USD rate?" but answers "What is an exchange rate?" directly. Your PM wants Claude to lean toward the tool more often. Which two statements match Anthropic's tool use overview?

choices.text: The tool must be misconfigured, because under `auto` a defined tool gets called on every single turn
choices.reason: With `auto`, Claude decides on each turn whether to call a tool or respond directly.

choices.text: Expected: stable knowledge gets a direct answer; requests needing the tool's capability call it
choices.reason: Correct: Claude calls a tool when the request maps to its described capability and the answer isn't in context; it answers stable knowledge directly.

choices.text: Adding `strict: true` to the tool definition makes Claude call the tool more often
choices.reason: Strict tool use makes calls match your schema exactly; it doesn't change when Claude decides to call.

choices.text: Shortening the tool description to a few words makes Claude reach for the tool more readily
choices.reason: Claude calls a tool when the request maps to its described capability; a thinner description gives it less to match against, not more.

choices.text: A system-prompt line like "Use the tools to investigate before responding." raises tool use
choices.reason: Correct: the boundary is steerable through the system prompt, and this light instruction increases tool use.

takeaway: Claude calls a tool when a request needs its described capability; steer how readily it does so with the system prompt.
explanation: Under `auto`, Claude weighs each request against each tool's described capability and answers general knowledge itself. The deciding detail is that only the live-data question triggered the tool, which is the documented behavior. Choice c is tempting because strict sounds like stricter tool use, but it governs input shape, not whether Claude calls the tool.

stem: Your AI application is an MCP host connected to three MCP servers: GitHub, a database and Sentry. According to MCP's architecture overview, how do the tools of all three servers reach the language model?

choices.text: The model connects to each server itself and sends `tools/list` whenever it needs a tool
choices.reason: The application, not the model, fetches tools through its MCP clients and later routes the model's calls to the right server.

choices.text: Only the first connected server's tools are offered, so that tool names can't clash
choices.reason: The application fetches available tools from all connected MCP servers, not only one of them.

choices.text: The app fetches tools from all connected servers and merges them into one tool registry
choices.reason: Correct: the application combines the tools from all connected servers into a unified tool registry that the model can access.

choices.text: Each server sends its tools to the model as resources, which the model reads before choosing one
choices.reason: Tools are discovered with `tools/list`; resources are a separate primitive for contextual data.

takeaway: The host gathers every server's tools into one registry for the model, then routes each call back to the right server.
explanation: In MCP the application sits between the model and the servers: its clients list each server's tools, and it hands the combined set to the model. The deciding detail is that three separate servers feed one model. Choice a is tempting because the model is the one choosing tools, but discovery and routing are the application's job.

diagram.caption: One MCP client per server inside the host.

stem: You replace your own MCP client with the MCP connector on the Messages API. Responses now contain `mcp_tool_use` and `mcp_tool_result` blocks, which your loop (written for `tool_use`) ignores. What do these blocks represent?

choices.text: Claude wants your app to run each MCP call and send back a `tool_result` for every `mcp_tool_use`
choices.reason: The connector connects to remote MCP servers without a separate MCP client; the result arrives in an `mcp_tool_result` block.

choices.text: The API called the remote server for you: one block is the call, the other its result
choices.reason: Correct: when Claude uses MCP tools through the connector, the response includes these two new content block types.

choices.text: The server failed to connect, so the call came back unexecuted for you to retry
choices.reason: These are the normal block types a response includes whenever Claude uses MCP tools, not error markers.

choices.text: They are web search `server_tool_use` blocks that get renamed whenever MCP servers are attached
choices.reason: They are the connector's own block types for MCP tool calls and results; `mcp_tool_use` even names the server.

takeaway: With the MCP connector, the API makes the MCP call: `mcp_tool_use` shows the call and `mcp_tool_result` its result.
explanation: The MCP connector moves the MCP client into the API, so connecting, calling and returning results happen without your code. The deciding detail is that you replaced your own client with the connector. Choice a is tempting because it matches how client tools work, but with the connector there's no MCP call for your app to run.

stem: With a Notion MCP server attached through the MCP connector, users ask "How do Notion databases work?" and Claude answers without calling any tool. A teammate files a bug saying the connector is broken. What is actually going on?

choices.text: The server's tools aren't enabled, because an `mcp_toolset` disables every tool by default
choices.reason: Every tool in a toolset is enabled by default (`enabled: true`); you opt into allowlisting with `default_config`.

choices.text: The connector only calls an MCP tool when the user names that tool explicitly in the request
choices.reason: Claude calls MCP tools explicitly or implicitly, such as "what's blocking the release?" with a Jira server attached.

choices.text: The question needs an MCP resource, and the connector only gives Claude MCP prompts
choices.reason: The connector currently supports only tool calls from the MCP feature set, not prompts or resources.

choices.text: Expected: general questions get direct answers; questions about your own data use tools
choices.reason: Correct: "how do Notion databases work?" is answered directly, while "what's in my Projects database?" triggers the tool.

takeaway: Connected MCP tools are for requests that need the service, not general-knowledge questions about it.
explanation: Claude calls an MCP tool when a request maps to the tool's described capability, which here means your Notion data. The deciding detail is that the question asks how Notion works in general. Choice a is tempting because no call looks like a configuration fault, but toolsets enable every tool by default.

stem: A teammate is summarizing MCP for a design review. Which two of their statements match MCP's architecture overview?

choices.text: MCP dictates how the AI application prompts its model and manages the context it receives
choices.reason: MCP focuses solely on the protocol for context exchange; it doesn't dictate how AI applications use LLMs or manage the context.

choices.text: Besides tools, servers can also expose resources (context data) and prompts (templates)
choices.reason: Correct: MCP defines three core server primitives: tools, resources and prompts.

choices.text: One MCP client inside the host keeps connections open to all of the host's servers
choices.reason: The host creates one MCP client for each MCP server, and each client maintains a dedicated connection.

choices.text: A tool's `inputSchema` is optional, since the model infers arguments from the description
choices.reason: Each tool object includes an `inputSchema`, a JSON Schema defining the expected input parameters.

choices.text: Clients discover tools with `tools/list`, then execute them with the `tools/call` method
choices.reason: Correct: clients use `*/list` methods to discover primitives, and `tools/call` executes a tool.

takeaway: MCP standardizes how servers offer tools, resources and prompts; how the app uses its model is left to the app.
explanation: MCP covers the exchange between clients and servers: discovering primitives with `*/list` and running tools with `tools/call`. The deciding detail in choice a is its claim about prompting and context management, which MCP explicitly leaves to the application. Choice c is tempting because one connection manager sounds simpler, but MCP uses one client per server.

stem: Your Agent SDK agent connects to a GitHub MCP server named `github`, and the init message shows it as `connected`. Claude can see `mcp__github__list_issues` among its tools but never manages to use it. What is the likely fix?

choices.text: Rename the server so that its tools lose the `mcp__` prefix that is blocking the calls
choices.reason: `mcp__<server-name>__<tool-name>` is the normal naming pattern for MCP tools, not something that blocks them.

choices.text: Switch the server from HTTP to stdio, because only local servers' tools can be called
choices.reason: The SDK supports stdio, HTTP/SSE and SDK MCP servers alike; the transport isn't what stops a connected server's tools.

choices.text: Allow it in `allowedTools`, e.g. `mcp__github__list_issues` or `mcp__github__*`
choices.reason: Correct: MCP tools require explicit permission. Without it, Claude sees that the tools are available but can't call them.

choices.text: Raise `MCP_TIMEOUT`, because the server's tool calls are running out of time
choices.reason: `MCP_TIMEOUT` is the connection limit, and the server is already connected; seen-but-unused tools point to missing permission.

takeaway: In the Agent SDK, connected MCP tools still need permission: allow them in `allowedTools` by their `mcp__server__tool` names.
explanation: Connecting a server makes its tools visible, but the SDK still requires explicit permission before Claude can use them. The deciding detail is that the server is `connected` and Claude can see the tool. Choice d is tempting because MCP problems often look like timeouts, but `MCP_TIMEOUT` governs connecting, which already succeeded.

source.title: Connect to external tools with MCP

stem: You're wiring three integrations into an Agent SDK agent: a server whose docs give a command (`npx @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem`), a vendor server whose docs give a URL, and tools you're writing in your own code. Which two pairings match the SDK's MCP guide?

choices.text: A command to run in the docs means connecting that server over stdio
choices.reason: Correct: if the docs give you a command to run, use stdio, which suits local processes on the same machine.

choices.text: Your own in-code tools should run as a separate stdio server process
choices.reason: For tools you build in code, use an SDK MCP server, which runs within your application instead of a separate process.

choices.text: Wrap the vendor's URL in a local stdio command before connecting to it
choices.reason: When the docs give you a URL, use HTTP or SSE; stdio is for local processes that talk over stdin/stdout.

choices.text: A URL in the docs means an HTTP or SSE server config for the vendor
choices.reason: Correct: if the docs give you a URL, use HTTP or SSE, which suit cloud-hosted servers and remote APIs.

choices.text: Run the filesystem command as an SDK MCP server inside your application
choices.reason: SDK MCP servers are for custom tools you define in your own code; a command to run means a stdio server.

takeaway: Command to run → stdio; URL → HTTP or SSE; tools in your own code → an SDK MCP server.
explanation: The SDK guide picks a transport from what the server's docs give you. The deciding details are the command for the filesystem server and the URL for the vendor. Choice b is tempting because your own tools are local too, but tools defined in your code run as an in-process SDK MCP server, not a separate stdio process.

source.title: Connect to external tools with MCP

stem: Your company wants its internal CRM usable from Claude, VS Code and Cursor. One plan writes separate tool schemas and handlers inside each app; the other builds a single MCP server. What does MCP's introduction say favors the server?

choices.text: MCP servers run inside the model, so the tools need no execution code at all
choices.reason: MCP is a standard for connecting AI applications to external systems; the server is one of those systems, not part of the model.

choices.text: Each client needs its own version of the MCP server, so the effort is the same either way
choices.reason: MCP is an open protocol supported across a wide range of clients, which makes it easy to build once and integrate everywhere.

choices.text: MCP only works with Claude, so the other apps would still need their hand-written schemas
choices.reason: MCP is supported by assistants like Claude and ChatGPT and by tools like Visual Studio Code and Cursor.

choices.text: It's an open protocol that many clients support: build once, integrate everywhere
choices.reason: Correct: because a wide range of clients support MCP, it is easy to build once and integrate everywhere.

takeaway: One MCP server can serve every MCP-capable client: build it once, integrate it everywhere.
explanation: MCP standardizes the connection between AI applications and external systems, so one server works with any client that speaks the protocol. The deciding detail is that the same CRM must reach three different apps. Choice b is tempting if you assume each app needs custom glue, but the shared protocol is what removes that work.

source.title: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

stem: Your team's MCP server already exposes tools for your ticketing system. Support leads now want a reusable "Weekly escalation report" workflow that users pick from their client's slash-command menu and fill in with a team name and date range. What should the server add?

choices.text: A prompt: a reusable template with arguments that the user invokes
choices.reason: Correct: prompts are pre-built, parameterized templates that are user-controlled, often exposed as slash commands.

choices.text: A tool named `weekly_report`, since tools are what users invoke from menus
choices.reason: Tools are model-controlled: the model decides when to call them based on user requests.

choices.text: A resource holding the report text, which the application loads as context
choices.reason: Resources are passive, read-only data sources that the application decides how to use; they aren't invoked workflows.

choices.text: A longer tool description that tells the model to produce the report weekly
choices.reason: Tool descriptions inform the model's choice of tools; an explicit, user-invoked template is what prompts provide.

takeaway: A workflow the **user** picks and fills in is an MCP **prompt**; tools are model-controlled, resources application-controlled.
explanation: MCP gives each building block a different controller: the model calls tools, the application chooses resources, and the user explicitly invokes prompts. A menu item users choose and fill with arguments is exactly a parameterized prompt. B is tempting because the server already has tools, but the model, not the user, decides when a tool runs.

stem: Your `book_flight` tool expects `passengers` as an integer. Now and then Claude sends `"2"` or leaves out a required field, and your booking code throws a runtime error. You want every call to match the schema without writing validate-and-retry code. What should you change?

choices.text: Set `strict: true` on the tool so its inputs follow the schema
choices.reason: Correct: strict tool use constrains sampling so the tool `input` strictly follows your `input_schema`, with correctly typed values.

choices.text: Add a line to the description saying `passengers` must be a number
choices.reason: Descriptions guide Claude but guarantee nothing; without strict mode Claude might still send `"2"` instead of `2`.

choices.text: Set `tool_choice` so Claude is forced to call `book_flight` each turn
choices.reason: Forcing a call isn't the problem here; strict mode is what makes the tool's inputs match the schema.

choices.text: Change `passengers` to a string so any value Claude sends is accepted
choices.reason: That hides the mismatch and moves parsing into your code; strict mode gives you a correctly typed integer instead.

takeaway: Need schema-valid tool inputs every time? Set **`strict: true`** on the tool: no more `"2"` for `2` or missing required fields.
explanation: Without strict mode, Claude might return incompatible types (`"2"` instead of `2`) or omit required fields, which breaks your functions. Setting **`strict: true`** constrains sampling so the tool input strictly follows your `input_schema` (A), so you don't need validate-and-retry code. B is the tempting trap: clearer descriptions help but guarantee nothing. C controls whether a tool is called, and D weakens the schema.

stem: Your `get_customer` tool returns the full database record: 60 fields, an internal UUID for every related object, and raw timestamps. Claude's answers about customers are slow and sometimes mix up related records. Which two changes does Anthropic's post on writing tools for agents suggest?

choices.text: Return every field, so Claude always has the complete record to reason over
choices.reason: The post advises returning only high-signal information to agents, not everything the backend holds.

choices.text: Add more UUIDs, so each related record can be referenced exactly
choices.reason: The post found that resolving arbitrary UUIDs into meaningful language improved precision by reducing hallucinations.

choices.text: Return only the high-signal fields Claude needs, not the whole record
choices.reason: Correct: tools should return only high-signal information back to agents.

choices.text: Return a bare status code, so the response costs as few tokens as possible
choices.reason: The post asks for meaningful, actionable context; opaque codes leave Claude without what it needs.

choices.text: Swap opaque IDs for meaningful names, or offer a concise/detailed `response_format`
choices.reason: Correct: interpretable names reduced hallucinations, and a `response_format` enum lets the agent choose concise or detailed output.

takeaway: Tool responses should be **high-signal**: only the fields Claude needs, with meaningful names instead of opaque IDs.
explanation: What a tool returns goes into Claude's context, so the post asks tools to return only **high-signal information** and to resolve low-level technical identifiers such as UUIDs into meaningful language (C, E). The stem's slow answers and mixed-up records point at bloated, opaque output. A is the tempting trap, assuming more data always helps. B adds more opaque IDs, and D swings too far, leaving Claude nothing useful.

source.title: Writing effective tools for agents — with agents

stem: Your app connects to an MCP server with read-only search tools and a `delete_record` tool. Users complain that they must approve every search, but deletions must still need a person's sign-off. Which approach matches MCP's guidance on user control over tools?

choices.text: Drop approvals entirely, because tools are model-controlled and the model knows best
choices.reason: Tools are model-controlled, but MCP emphasizes human oversight, such as approval dialogs for tool executions.

choices.text: Convert `delete_record` into a resource, so the application decides when it runs
choices.reason: Resources are passive, read-only data sources; deleting a record is an action, which is what tools are for.

choices.text: Pre-approve the safe read-only searches and keep an approval step for each deletion
choices.reason: Correct: applications can pre-approve certain safe operations in permission settings and use approval dialogs for individual executions.

choices.text: Convert the search tools into prompts, so users start each search themselves
choices.reason: Prompts are user-invoked templates; making searches prompts stops the model from searching when it needs to.

takeaway: Match oversight to risk: **pre-approve safe operations**, keep **per-call approval** for actions with side effects.
explanation: MCP tools are model-controlled, so the application supplies human oversight: approval dialogs for individual executions, and permission settings that pre-approve safe operations. Searches are read-only, while deletions change data, so only deletions keep the approval step. A is tempting because it removes the friction, but it also removes the sign-off that deletions require.

stem: Your API app must answer questions using current information from the public web. The team doesn't want to build, host or run any search infrastructure. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: A user-defined `search_web` tool whose handler calls a search provider
choices.reason: With a user-defined tool, your application executes every call and runs the loop: the infrastructure the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: Anthropic's `bash` tool, so Claude can fetch search pages with shell commands
choices.reason: `bash` is client-executed: Anthropic publishes the schema, but your application runs each command.

choices.text: No tool at all, since Claude can answer from what it learned in training
choices.reason: Fresh or external data, such as current information, is outside the training data and needs a tool to fetch it.

choices.text: Anthropic's `web_search` server tool, which Anthropic runs for you
choices.reason: Correct: server-executed tools such as web search run on Anthropic's side; you enable the tool and read the results.

takeaway: When a **server tool** already does the job, enable it: Anthropic runs it, and you don't host anything.
explanation: Tools differ mainly in where the code runs. User-defined and Anthropic-schema tools such as `bash` run in your application, while server tools such as `web_search` run on Anthropic's infrastructure. The constraint "no search infrastructure" points to the server tool. A is tempting because a custom tool gives full control, but your code would have to execute every search.

stem: Your project CLAUDE.md has grown to 500 lines, and Claude has started missing some of its rules. A teammate proposes moving half of it into separate files pulled in with `@path` imports, so Claude loads less. What will that change actually do?

choices.text: The imported files will load only when Claude works with a file in the same directory
choices.reason: That describes CLAUDE.md files in subdirectories, which load on demand. Imported files are expanded and loaded at launch with the file that imports them.

choices.text: It organizes the file, but imported files still load at launch, so the context cost stays the same
choices.reason: Correct: imports help you organize a long file but don't reduce its context cost, because imported files also load at launch.

choices.text: Imported content becomes enforced configuration, so Claude can no longer skip those rules
choices.reason: Claude treats CLAUDE.md content as context, not enforced configuration; to block an action regardless, the docs point to a PreToolUse hook.

choices.text: Claude will load each imported file only when it judges the file relevant, as it does with skills
choices.reason: That's how skills behave. Imports load at launch; to load content only when needed, use path-scoped rules or skills.

takeaway: `@path` imports tidy a long CLAUDE.md but don't shrink it: trim it, or move content into path-scoped rules or skills.
explanation: Size hurts adherence because everything that loads at launch competes for attention, so the fix has to change what loads at launch. Imports only change where the text lives; the stem's goal of loading less is not met. Choice d is tempting because skills do load on demand, but imported files are expanded into context at launch alongside the CLAUDE.md that references them.

stem: You ran `/init` in an existing repo, and it generated a starter CLAUDE.md. Before committing it, you review each entry by asking whether removing it would cause Claude to make mistakes. Which entries should stay in CLAUDE.md?

choices.text: A file-by-file description of every module under `src/`
choices.reason: The best-practices guide lists file-by-file descriptions, and anything Claude can figure out by reading code, as things to exclude.

choices.text: "Run tests with `make test-unit`, not plain `pytest`"
choices.reason: Correct: Bash commands Claude can't guess and preferred test runners are on the guide's include list.

choices.text: "Write clean, readable, well-structured code"
choices.reason: Self-evident practices like "write clean code" are on the exclude list; they don't change what Claude does.

choices.text: The full reference docs for the internal billing API
choices.reason: Detailed API documentation is excluded (link to docs instead); knowledge needed only sometimes belongs in a skill.

choices.text: "Set `APP_ENV=local` before starting the dev server"
choices.reason: Correct: developer environment quirks such as required env vars are on the include list; Claude can't infer them.

takeaway: Treat an `/init` draft as a baseline: keep what Claude can't guess, cut what it can read from the code or already knows.
explanation: CLAUDE.md loads every session, so each line should change Claude's behavior. The test command and the env var are things Claude can't infer from the code. Choice d is tempting because the billing API is project-specific, but detailed reference docs bloat every session; link to them, or move them into a skill that loads on demand.

stem: Your root CLAUDE.md says to write tests with Jest. A `packages/web/CLAUDE.md` written last year says to use Vitest. When Claude works in `packages/web/`, it sometimes uses one framework and sometimes the other. What explains this, and what's the fix?

choices.text: The subdirectory file should override the root file, so it's a loading bug; restart the session
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md files don't override each other: all discovered files are concatenated into context.

choices.text: The root file always wins because it loads first, so move the Vitest instruction into it
choices.reason: Load order doesn't make a file win. Contradicting instructions let Claude pick either one, wherever they live.

choices.text: Nested CLAUDE.md files are ignored unless imported, so add an `@` import for the subdirectory file
choices.reason: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load on demand, once Claude reads, writes or edits a file in that subdirectory.

choices.text: The two files contradict each other, so Claude may pick either; remove the outdated instruction
choices.reason: Correct: if two instructions contradict each other, Claude may pick one arbitrarily. Review instruction files to remove outdated or conflicting ones.

takeaway: CLAUDE.md files are combined, not ranked: contradictions make Claude's choice arbitrary, so prune outdated instructions.
explanation: Both files reach Claude's context when it works in `packages/web/`, and nothing ranks one above the other, so the inconsistent behavior comes from the contradiction itself. The fix is to remove the stale line. Choice a is tempting because nested settings often override parents, but CLAUDE.md files are concatenated rather than overriding each other.

stem: You added `.claude/rules/frontend.md` with `paths: ["src/web/**"]` in its frontmatter. Right after launch, the rule isn't in Claude's context, and a teammate thinks it's broken. When will it load?

choices.text: When Claude reads, writes or edits a file that matches `src/web/**`
choices.reason: Correct: a path-scoped rule loads when Claude uses Read, Write or Edit on a matching file, or views one with a Bash read such as `cat`.

choices.text: Only after you import it from CLAUDE.md with an `@.claude/rules/frontend.md` line
choices.reason: No import is needed: every `.md` file in `.claude/rules/` is discovered automatically, recursively.

choices.text: Only in sessions that you launch from inside the `src/web/` directory itself
choices.reason: A path-scoped rule is triggered by Claude working with a matching file, not by the directory you launch from.

choices.text: When you open `/memory` and switch the rule on for the current session
choices.reason: `/memory` opens your memory files for viewing and editing; it isn't a switch that loads path-scoped rules.

takeaway: A rule with `paths` stays out of context until Claude works with a matching file; that's the point of scoping it.
explanation: Rules without `paths` load at launch; adding `paths` makes a rule conditional on Claude touching a matching file. So the rule isn't broken: it is waiting for the first read, write or edit under `src/web/`. Choice b is tempting because imports pull files into CLAUDE.md, but rules in `.claude/rules/` are discovered on their own.

stem: A teammate says path-scoped rules and skills are interchangeable, because both keep instructions out of context until they're needed. Which difference should guide which one you pick?

choices.text: Skills load at launch in every session, while rules wait until someone invokes them
choices.reason: This is inverted: skills load when invoked or judged relevant, and rules load every session or when matching files are opened.

choices.text: Rules can live only in `~/.claude/rules/`, so they can't be shared with the team
choices.reason: Project rules live in the repo's `.claude/rules/`, which keeps team instructions modular and easier to maintain.

choices.text: Rules load when Claude works with matching files; skills load when invoked or judged relevant
choices.reason: Correct: rules load every session or when matching files are opened; skills load when you invoke them or Claude judges them relevant to your prompt.

choices.text: Rules are enforced on every tool call, while skills are only suggestions Claude may ignore
choices.reason: Rules are instructions loaded into context, like CLAUDE.md, not enforcement; to block an action regardless, the docs point to a PreToolUse hook.

takeaway: Pick a rule when guidance follows the files being touched; pick a skill when it follows the task being done.
explanation: Both mechanisms save context, but their triggers differ: a path-scoped rule is tied to which files Claude works with, while a skill is tied to the task and loads when invoked or judged relevant. That makes rules fit directory- or file-type guidance and skills fit task-specific workflows. Choice d is tempting because rules sound strict, but they are context, not enforcement.

stem: Your personal `~/.claude/rules/style.md` says to indent with tabs. The project's `.claude/rules/style.md` says to use 2-space indentation. Claude's indentation in this repo is inconsistent. What does the memory guide say about this situation?

choices.text: Project rules override user rules, the same way project settings override user settings
choices.reason: Rules don't follow settings precedence: user rules load before project rules, but neither set overrides the other.

choices.text: Neither set overrides the other, so Claude may follow either; keep them consistent
choices.reason: Correct: if a user rule and a project rule conflict, Claude may follow either one, so the guide says to keep them consistent.

choices.text: User rules always win, because your personal preferences outrank the project's
choices.reason: No set wins. Both load, and a conflict leaves Claude free to follow either instruction.

choices.text: Only one `style.md` loads, because rule files with the same name replace each other
choices.reason: Both sets load: Claude Code loads user-level rules first, then project rules, so both instructions reach Claude.

takeaway: User and project rules are both loaded and neither wins a conflict, so contradictions between them make behavior unpredictable.
explanation: Rules files add instructions to Claude's context; they don't merge by precedence like settings do. Both `style.md` files load, user rules first, so Claude sees two contradicting indentation rules and may follow either. Choice a is tempting because settings do have a precedence order, but the guide says neither set of rules overrides the other.

stem: After an hour of discussion in your main Claude Code session, Claude delegates a refactor to your custom `refactorer` subagent (not a fork). Which of these are in the subagent's context when it starts?

choices.text: The main conversation's history, so it knows what you discussed
choices.reason: A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context and doesn't see your conversation history; it works from Claude's delegation message.

choices.text: The files Claude has already read in the main conversation
choices.reason: Files Claude already read don't carry over; the subagent reads what it needs in its own context.

choices.text: The project's CLAUDE.md files, which custom subagents load
choices.reason: Correct: a non-fork subagent loads every level of the CLAUDE.md hierarchy the main conversation loads, unless its definition sets `omitClaudeMd`.

choices.text: The skills you already invoked in the main conversation
choices.reason: Skills invoked in the main conversation don't carry over; only skills listed in its `skills` field are preloaded.

choices.text: Its own system prompt, from its definition's markdown body
choices.reason: Correct: the markdown body of a custom subagent's file becomes its system prompt, plus environment details Claude Code appends.

takeaway: A non-fork subagent gets its own prompt, the task message and CLAUDE.md, but none of your conversation, files read or invoked skills.
explanation: Context isolation is what keeps a subagent's work out of your main window, and it cuts both ways: what lived only in your conversation doesn't reach the subagent. It still gets durable context, its own system prompt and the CLAUDE.md hierarchy. Choice d is tempting because the skills feel like part of the session, but only the `skills` field preloads them.

stem: In chat, your team agreed to keep the legacy `/v1` endpoints, and Claude saved this to auto memory. Later, your custom `cleanup` subagent (not a fork) deletes the `/v1` routes. Which change makes the decision reach this subagent, and future ones, every time they start?

choices.text: Write the decision into the project CLAUDE.md, which these subagents load on start
choices.reason: Correct: a non-fork subagent loads the CLAUDE.md hierarchy the main conversation loads, so the decision reaches every run.

choices.text: Leave it in auto memory, since subagents read the main conversation's saved memory notes
choices.reason: The main conversation's auto memory isn't loaded into a non-fork subagent; subagents need their own `memory` field.

choices.text: Restate the decision in the main chat so that it sits in the most recent turns
choices.reason: A non-fork subagent doesn't see your conversation history, however recent the turn.

choices.text: Set an output style for the session that states the decision in its instructions
choices.reason: A subagent runs its own system prompt, so your output style doesn't shape its responses, except in a fork.

takeaway: Decisions that must reach subagents need durable context, such as CLAUDE.md; chat, auto memory and output style stay with the main session.
explanation: A non-fork subagent starts fresh, so the question is which context it still loads. The CLAUDE.md hierarchy is on that list; conversation history, the main session's auto memory and its output style are not. Choice b is tempting because auto memory feels durable, but it belongs to the main conversation and isn't loaded into subagents.

stem: Your custom `security-auditor` subagent must never invoke a skill during its runs. A teammate says that leaving the `skills` field out of its frontmatter is enough. What do the subagent docs say?

choices.text: That's enough: a subagent without a `skills` field can't see or use any skill
choices.reason: The `skills` field controls preloading, not access: without it, a subagent can still discover and invoke skills through the Skill tool.

choices.text: Set `skills: []` in its frontmatter, which revokes access to every skill
choices.reason: The `skills` field only decides which skills are preloaded; an empty list preloads nothing but leaves the Skill tool available.

choices.text: Add `disable-model-invocation: true` to the subagent's own frontmatter
choices.reason: `disable-model-invocation` is a skill's frontmatter field that stops Claude invoking that skill; it isn't how you limit a subagent.

choices.text: Leave `Skill` out of its `tools` list, or add it to `disallowedTools`
choices.reason: Correct: to prevent a subagent from invoking skills entirely, omit `Skill` from `tools` or add it to `disallowedTools`.

takeaway: The `skills` field preloads skill content; access to skills is controlled by whether the subagent has the Skill tool.
explanation: Two separate controls are in play: which skills are injected at startup, and whether the subagent can invoke skills at all. The `skills` field handles the first; the tool list handles the second. Choice a is tempting because subagents don't inherit skills you invoked, but without the field they can still discover and invoke project, user and plugin skills.

stem: Your 400-line CLAUDE.md mixes three things: the project's build command, a rule that ESLint must run after every file edit, and a 30-step release checklist used once a month. Which reorganization gives each concern the right mechanism?

choices.text: Keep all three in CLAUDE.md, and mark the ESLint and release lines as IMPORTANT
choices.reason: The checklist would still load every session, and an ESLint instruction still relies on Claude; something that must run every time needs a hook.

choices.text: The build command in a skill, the ESLint rule in CLAUDE.md, the checklist in a hook
choices.reason: This swaps the roles: the build command is an always-needed convention, and a hook runs on events rather than holding a procedure.

choices.text: Build command in CLAUDE.md, ESLint as a file-edit hook, the checklist as a skill
choices.reason: Correct: CLAUDE.md is for conventions and build commands, a hook for automation on every matching event, a skill for repeatable workflows.

choices.text: Move all three into a subagent so that they stay out of the main conversation
choices.reason: A subagent is an isolated worker that returns a summary; it doesn't guide the main session or run on every edit.

takeaway: Always-needed facts go in CLAUDE.md, must-happen actions in hooks, and occasional procedures in skills.
explanation: Each concern has a different trigger: the build command is needed in every session, ESLint must run on every edit without Claude choosing to, and the checklist matters once a month. Those map to CLAUDE.md, a hook and a skill. Choice a is tempting because it changes nothing structural, but emphasis doesn't make an instruction run every time or stop the checklist loading every session.

stem: A teammate wrote a `SessionStart` hook that only echoes the same fixed list of team coding conventions into every session. Nothing in the list changes from one session to the next. What does the hooks reference suggest instead?

choices.text: Switch it to a `UserPromptSubmit` hook so the list is repeated before every prompt
choices.reason: That adds the same text before every prompt. For static context that doesn't need a script, the reference points to CLAUDE.md.

choices.text: Put the fixed conventions in CLAUDE.md, and keep SessionStart for dynamic context
choices.reason: Correct: SessionStart suits context like existing issues or recent changes; for static context that doesn't require a script, use CLAUDE.md.

choices.text: Keep the hook, because SessionStart is the only way to add context at session start
choices.reason: It isn't the only route: the reference itself recommends CLAUDE.md for static context that needs no script.

choices.text: Move the list into a `SessionEnd` hook so it's saved for the next session
choices.reason: `SessionEnd` runs when a session ends, for tasks like cleanup or logging; it doesn't put anything into the next session's context.

takeaway: Static, always-true context belongs in CLAUDE.md; a `SessionStart` hook earns its place when the context has to be generated.
explanation: Hooks are for things a script must do; a fixed list doesn't need one, and CLAUDE.md already loads at the start of every session. SessionStart stays useful for context that changes, such as open issues or recent changes. Choice c is tempting because the hook does work, but it isn't the only route, and the reference points static context to CLAUDE.md.

stem: You wrote a `changelog` skill in `~/.claude/skills/changelog/`, and Claude Code uses it in every project on your laptop. A teammate who cloned the same repository can't see it at all. What explains this, and what's the fix?

choices.text: Personal skills load only for you; move it to the repo's `.claude/skills/` and commit it
choices.reason: Correct: `~/.claude/skills/` loads in all your projects on this machine, while `.claude/skills/` in the repository loads for the repo, so committing it gives the team the skill too.

choices.text: Skills load only for the person who wrote them, so each teammate must write their own copy
choices.reason: Where you save a skill decides which sessions load it. A skill committed to the repository's `.claude/skills/` reaches everyone who works there.

choices.text: The teammate has to invoke `/changelog` by name once before Claude Code can discover it
choices.reason: Invoking by name doesn't change discovery. The skill isn't in any location the teammate's sessions load, so there's nothing to invoke.

choices.text: Claude Code shares skills only after they're uploaded, so upload it for your teammates
choices.reason: Claude Code skills are files on disk: saving one under the repository's `.claude/skills/` and committing it is what shares it.

takeaway: In Claude Code, a skill's location sets its reach: `~/.claude/skills/` is yours everywhere; a committed `.claude/skills/` reaches the team.
explanation: Claude Code discovers skills from the filesystem, and the folder decides who gets them. The detail that decides it is the path: `~/.claude/skills/` sits in your home directory, so only your sessions load it. Choice c is tempting because skills can be invoked by name, but invoking doesn't help when the teammate's sessions never load the file.

stem: Your Messages API app uses a custom skill whose script reads a pricing file from a folder on your application server. In testing, the script can't find the file. Where does a skill attached to a Messages API request actually run?

choices.text: In your application's own process, so the script should read your server's file paths directly
choices.reason: API skills don't run in your application. They run in the code execution environment, so your server's folders aren't there.

choices.text: On the end user's device, which downloads the skill along with each response
choices.reason: Nothing runs on the user's device. Skills named in the request's `container` run in the code execution environment.

choices.text: In the code execution container, apart from your app; send input files with the Files API
choices.reason: Correct: skills run in the code execution environment. To give a skill files to work on, upload them with the Files API and reference them with a container upload block.

choices.text: In a copy of Claude Code on your server, which the API calls to run the skill's scripts
choices.reason: The API doesn't call out to Claude Code. Skills specified in the `container` parameter run in the code execution environment.

takeaway: On the Messages API a skill runs in the code execution container, not your app; pass files in with the Files API.
explanation: A skill on the API runs in the code execution container, so your server's folders aren't visible to it. The script's failure to find a file on your server is the clue. Choice a is tempting because the app makes the request, but making the request doesn't put the skill in your process; input files must be uploaded and referenced instead.

diagram.caption: The skill runs in the container, so files reach it by upload.

source.title: Using Agent Skills with the API

stem: A skill that works well in Claude Code calls your company's public REST API with `curl` and runs `pip install` for a helper library at the start of each run. You upload the same skill for a Messages API app. What should you expect?

choices.text: It runs unchanged, since a skill behaves the same way on every surface that supports it
choices.reason: The runtime depends on the surface. Claude Code skills have the user's network access; API skills don't, so the same steps behave differently.

choices.text: Those steps fail: API skills have no network access and can't install packages at runtime
choices.reason: Correct: on the Claude API, skills can't make external API calls or install new packages; only pre-installed packages are available.

choices.text: It runs once the skill is also uploaded in claude.ai, which grants it network access on the API
choices.reason: Custom skills don't sync across surfaces, and a claude.ai upload doesn't change the API's runtime, which has no network access.

choices.text: It runs if the skill's description names the REST API and the library it installs
choices.reason: The description decides when Claude triggers the skill. It doesn't change what the runtime allows, and API skills have no network access.

takeaway: Plan each skill for its runtime: on the Claude API there's no network access and no runtime package install.
explanation: A skill's format is portable, but its runtime isn't: the API container has no network access and only pre-installed packages. The `curl` call and the `pip install` are exactly the two things the API runtime blocks. Choice a is tempting because the same SKILL.md loads everywhere, but loading isn't the same as running, and Claude Code's network access doesn't carry over.

stem: Your Agent SDK service sets `settingSources: []` so that settings files on the machine can't affect it. Since then, Claude never uses the project skills in the repo's `.claude/skills/`, even for requests that clearly match their descriptions. What's the cause?

choices.text: The SDK doesn't support skills at all; they work only in interactive Claude Code sessions
choices.reason: The SDK does support skills: it discovers them from the filesystem, and Claude invokes them when relevant or you dispatch them by name.

choices.text: Skills must first be registered in code with an SDK call before Claude can see any of them
choices.reason: The SDK has no programmatic API for registering skills. You create them as `SKILL.md` files on disk, which the SDK discovers.

choices.text: The SDK matches descriptions more strictly than the CLI does, so they all need rewriting
choices.reason: The descriptions already match. With no setting sources, the SDK doesn't load skills at all, whatever their descriptions say.

choices.text: Skills load through setting sources; include `'project'` (and `'user'` for personal skills)
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK discovers skills through the user and project setting sources. If you set `settingSources` explicitly and omit them, it doesn't load skills.

takeaway: In the Agent SDK, skills are files discovered through setting sources; leave out `'project'` and project skills don't load.
explanation: The SDK loads skills from the filesystem, and `settingSources` decides which filesystem locations it reads. The deciding detail is the empty list: it switches off the user and project sources that skills come from. Choice b is tempting because subagents can be defined in code, but skills can't; they're always files on disk.

stem: You're moving a report-writing workflow to Claude Managed Agents. The workflow's skill currently lives only in your laptop's `~/.claude/skills/` folder. How does the agent get the skill?

choices.text: Upload it to your workspace as a custom skill and list its ID in the agent's `skills` array
choices.reason: Correct: you upload a custom skill (a directory with `SKILL.md`) to your workspace, which returns a `skill_*` ID, and attach it in the agent's `skills` array.

choices.text: Anthropic scans your laptop's `~/.claude/skills/` folder each time a session starts
choices.reason: Skills reach a Managed Agent through its `skills` array or a mounted GitHub repository's `.claude/skills`, not from folders on your laptop.

choices.text: Send the skill's name in a user event, and the agent then fetches the skill from your machine
choices.reason: The agent invokes attached skills automatically when relevant. It doesn't fetch skills from your machine; they come from the `skills` array or a mounted repo.

choices.text: Install it in Claude Code as a plugin, since Managed Agents loads your enabled plugins
choices.reason: Skills reach a Managed Agent in two ways, the agent's `skills` array or a mounted GitHub repository. Claude Code plugins aren't one of them.

takeaway: A Managed Agent gets skills from its definition: upload custom skills to the workspace and list them in the agent's `skills` array.
explanation: In Managed Agents the agent is an API resource, and its skills are part of that definition. The deciding detail is that the skill lives only on your laptop, which Anthropic's infrastructure never reads. Choice b is tempting because Claude Code discovers that very folder, but Managed Agents has no discovery step on your machine.

stem: Your team wants one `invoice-check` skill to work in Claude Code, in a Messages API app and in Claude Managed Agents. Which two authoring practices from Anthropic's skill best practices help it work everywhere?

choices.text: Write the `description` to say what the skill does and when Claude should use it
choices.reason: Correct: the description is how Claude discovers and selects the skill, so it must say both what the skill does and when to use it.

choices.text: Use backslash paths such as `scripts\check.py`, which every platform accepts
choices.reason: Use forward slashes (`scripts/check.py`). Windows-style paths cause errors on Unix systems; Unix-style paths work across all platforms.

choices.text: Install any packages the skill needs at the start of each run, on every surface it runs on
choices.reason: The Claude API has no network access and no runtime package installation, so installing at run time fails there.

choices.text: Put the full procedure in the `description` so it's always in context everywhere
choices.reason: The description is for selection: what the skill does and when to use it. The rest of SKILL.md holds the implementation details.

choices.text: List the packages the skill needs, and check they're available where it runs
choices.reason: Correct: list required packages in SKILL.md and verify they're available in the code execution tool documentation.

takeaway: A portable skill describes its trigger clearly and doesn't assume tools or packages exist wherever it runs.
explanation: Portability comes from two habits: a description that works as the matching criterion, and a body that doesn't assume a particular machine. A trigger-focused description helps on every surface, and checking packages protects against runtimes like the API's. Choice c is tempting because it works in Claude Code, but the API container can't install packages at run time.

stem: Your team enables two plugins, `payments` and `docs`. Each one ships a skill named `review`. What happens when both plugins load?

choices.text: The plugin installed second overrides the first one, so only one `review` skill can run
choices.reason: Neither overrides the other. Plugin skills get the plugin's name as a prefix, so both can provide a `review` skill.

choices.text: Claude Code refuses to load either plugin until one of the skills is renamed
choices.reason: No rename is needed: the plugin-name prefix lets two plugins each provide a skill with the same name without colliding.

choices.text: Both load, as `/payments:review` and `/docs:review`, since plugin skills are namespaced
choices.reason: Correct: plugin skills get the plugin name as a prefix, such as `/my-plugin:hello`, so two plugins can each provide a skill without colliding.

choices.text: They merge into a single `/review` skill that runs both plugins' steps one after the other
choices.reason: Skills don't merge. Each plugin's skill keeps its own steps and runs under its own prefixed name.

takeaway: Plugin skills are namespaced as `/plugin-name:skill-name`, so same-named skills from different plugins don't collide.
explanation: Claude Code prefixes every plugin skill with its plugin's name. That's why the shared name `review` causes no conflict: the two skills become `/payments:review` and `/docs:review`. Choice a is tempting because it's how name clashes work in many systems, but namespacing means neither plugin has to win.

stem: Your project has 25 skills that are manual procedures, such as `/release` and `/rotate-keys`, which people only ever run by typing them. Their descriptions still take up Claude's context on every turn. Which change fits?

choices.text: Delete each skill's `description` field, which takes the skill out of Claude's context
choices.reason: Without a `description`, Claude Code uses the first non-empty line of the skill's content instead, so something still describes it.

choices.text: Set `user-invocable: false`, which keeps the skills out of Claude's context
choices.reason: That does the opposite: it hides the skill from the `/` menu so only Claude invokes it, and its description stays in context.

choices.text: Move the 25 procedures into CLAUDE.md, which loads only when it's needed
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md isn't loaded on demand. Skills are the mechanism whose full content loads only when invoked.

choices.text: Set `disable-model-invocation: true`, so each loads only when someone runs it
choices.reason: Correct: with this setting you can still invoke the skill, Claude can't on its own, and its description isn't in context until the full skill loads on invoke.

takeaway: `disable-model-invocation: true` turns a skill into a manual entry point: you run it, Claude doesn't, and its description leaves context.
explanation: Manual-only skills don't need Claude to know about them in advance, and `disable-model-invocation: true` removes them from Claude's view until a person runs them. The deciding detail is that people only ever type these procedures. Choice b is tempting because it also limits who invokes a skill, but it limits the other side and leaves the description in context.

stem: Your team keeps five internal Claude Code plugins in one Git repository. Teammates should be able to add that repository once, install any of the plugins by name and receive updates. What do you add to the repository?

choices.text: One `plugin.json` manifest at the repository root that names all five plugins
choices.reason: A `plugin.json` is one plugin's manifest, giving that plugin its name. Listing several plugins and where to fetch them is a marketplace's job.

choices.text: A `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` catalog listing each plugin and where to fetch it
choices.reason: Correct: a marketplace is a repository or directory with `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`. You add it once, then install plugins from it by name.

choices.text: A listing on Claude Marketplace, the claude.com site, that points to the repository
choices.reason: Claude Marketplace is a website for browsing plugins and connectors. It isn't a marketplace you add with `/plugin marketplace add`.

choices.text: An MCP server that hands the five plugins to Claude Code whenever it requests one
choices.reason: MCP servers are a plugin component that give Claude tools. They don't serve plugins; a marketplace lists them.

takeaway: A marketplace is a catalog file (`marketplace.json`) listing plugins; teammates add it once and install from it by name.
explanation: Distribution is the marketplace's job: it's a catalog, not a hosted store, that tells Claude Code which plugins exist and where to fetch each. The deciding needs are "add once", "install by name" and "updates". Choice c is tempting because of the name, but Claude Marketplace is a website, not a plugin catalog you register.

stem: Your team wrote a custom spreadsheet-reporting skill and wants Claude to use it inside your Messages API app. According to the API's skills guide, how do you make the skill available in a request?

choices.text: Upload it via the Skills API, then name its `skill_id` in `container` with code execution on
choices.reason: Correct: you upload a custom skill to your workspace, then specify it in the `container` parameter by `skill_id`; skills require the code execution tool.

choices.text: Save SKILL.md in a `.claude/skills/` folder on your server for the API to discover
choices.reason: The API doesn't scan your server. Skills are specified in the request's `container` parameter by `skill_id`, after a custom one is uploaded.

choices.text: Define it as a user-defined tool whose `description` holds the SKILL.md text
choices.reason: Skills go in the `container` parameter, not `tools`. The `tools` array carries the code execution tool that the skills run in.

choices.text: Upload SKILL.md with the Files API and attach it to each request with a container upload block
choices.reason: The Files API is for the input files a skill works on. The skill itself is uploaded through the Skills API to your workspace.

takeaway: On the API, upload a custom skill once, then name its `skill_id` in `container` alongside the code execution tool.
explanation: API skills are sent with the request, not discovered: you upload the skill to your workspace, then reference it in the `container` parameter, and it runs in the code execution container. The phrase "inside your Messages API app" rules out filesystem discovery. Choice d is tempting because files do travel through the Files API, but that path is for inputs, not for the skill.

source.title: Using Agent Skills with the API

stem: Developers use an `invoice-check` skill from your repo's `.claude/skills/` in Claude Code, and a product manager also uploaded it in claude.ai settings. Your new Messages API app expects Claude to use the same skill, but it never does. The app's requests reference no skills. What's the fix?

choices.text: Share the product manager's claude.ai skill with the organization so every surface gets it
choices.reason: claude.ai custom skills are individual to each user and can't be shared org-wide, and skills don't sync to the API from there.

choices.text: Make the skill's description more specific so the API picks up the copy in the repository
choices.reason: The description controls when a loaded skill triggers. The API never loads the repo's copy, because Claude Code skills are separate from the API.
