choices.text: Commit the skill to the app's repo too, since the API reads `.claude/skills/` from the caller
choices.reason: Claude Code skills are filesystem-based and separate from the API. The API uses skills named by `skill_id` in the request.

choices.text: Upload it through the Skills API and reference it in the app's requests; surfaces don't sync
choices.reason: Correct: custom skills don't sync across surfaces. API skills are uploaded through the Skills API and named by `skill_id` in the request.

takeaway: Custom skills don't sync between Claude Code, claude.ai and the API; set the skill up separately on each surface.
explanation: One SKILL.md can serve every surface, but each surface has its own store: the filesystem for Claude Code, Settings for claude.ai, and the Skills API for the API. The clue is that the app's requests name no skills, so the API has nothing to load. Choice c is tempting because filesystem discovery works in Claude Code, but the API never scans a repository.

diagram.caption: Three surfaces, three separate places to set up a custom skill.

stem: You're deciding how to package several Claude Code workflows. Which two statements match the Claude Code plugin guide?

choices.text: A `/deploy` procedure run only when someone types it: set `disable-model-invocation: true`
choices.reason: Correct: that frontmatter line means Claude doesn't run the skill on its own, so it runs only when invoked by name.

choices.text: Conventions Claude should apply on its own whenever relevant: set `disable-model-invocation: true`
choices.reason: That setting stops Claude running the skill on its own. Leave it out for a skill you want Claude to apply when relevant.

choices.text: A skill only you use, in one project, must be packaged as a plugin before it will load
choices.reason: Skills work standalone in your project or home directory. Keep the standalone setup while it serves one project or only you.

choices.text: Skills, agents and hooks to share with teammates across several projects: make a plugin
choices.reason: Correct: make a plugin when you want to share the setup with teammates, install it in several projects, or publish versioned releases.

choices.text: A plugin has to be listed in a marketplace before Claude Code can load it at all
choices.reason: You don't need a marketplace to run a plugin you're writing: load it from disk or a URL, for example with `--plugin-dir`.

takeaway: Standalone skill for you or one project; manual-only skill for a typed procedure; plugin to share a setup across teammates and projects.
explanation: The packaging choice follows who needs the workflow and who should trigger it. A procedure with side effects needs an explicit entry point, and a setup shared across teammates and projects needs a plugin. Choice c is tempting because plugins are the sharing mechanism, but a skill that serves only you or one project works fine standalone.

stem: Your Managed Agents sessions mount your GitHub repository, and the agent uses skills from its root `.claude/skills/`. Midway through a long session you push an improved version of one skill. The agent keeps following the old steps. Why, and what should you do?

choices.text: Skills are cached for a day after first use, so wait for the cache to expire
choices.reason: There's no such cache. The repository's skills are scanned once, when the session starts, so a new session is what picks up changes.

choices.text: The repo is scanned once at session start; start a new session to load the update
choices.reason: Correct: the scan runs once when the session starts, and commits pushed mid-session aren't picked up. Start a new session to load updated skills.

choices.text: Repo skills need an entry in the agent's `skills` array before updates can load
choices.reason: Repository skills need no upload and no entry in the agent's `skills` array; the issue is that the scan happens only at session start.

choices.text: Send an event asking the agent to re-read the skills folder, which pulls the commit
choices.reason: Commits pushed mid-session aren't picked up, and the scan runs only when a session starts. Start a new session to load updated skills.

takeaway: Managed Agents scan a mounted repo's `.claude/skills/` once per session; new sessions pick up skill changes.
explanation: Repository skills are discovered server-side when a session starts, from the checked-out state of the repo. The deciding detail is that you pushed mid-session, after that scan. Choice d is tempting because you can steer an agent with events, but commits pushed mid-session aren't picked up; only a new session loads them.

stem: Your GitHub MCP server is connected in Claude Code and exposes issues as resources. You want issue #123 in Claude's context when the turn starts, instead of waiting for Claude to decide to look it up. What should you do?

choices.text: Set `alwaysLoad: true` on the GitHub server so that its issues load into context at startup
choices.reason: `alwaysLoad` makes a server's tool definitions load upfront instead of through tool search; it doesn't put the server's data into context.

choices.text: Reference the issue in your prompt with an @ mention, the same way you reference a file
choices.reason: Correct: MCP resources can be referenced with @ mentions, and referenced resources are automatically fetched and included as attachments.

choices.text: Ask Claude to call the server's issue tool, because tools are the only way MCP data reaches Claude
choices.reason: Servers can also expose resources, which you reference directly with an @ mention; no tool call is needed to bring them in.

choices.text: Run one of the server's prompts as a command so that every open issue loads before you type
choices.reason: MCP prompts become commands whose result is injected into the conversation; they don't preload a server's data.

takeaway: Known data you want in context from the start is a **resource**: @-mention it and Claude Code fetches and attaches it.
explanation: A resource is data a server exposes for the client to fetch into context directly, rather than having the model call a tool to get it. The deciding detail is that you already know which issue you need. Choice a is tempting because it sounds like preloading, but `alwaysLoad` is about tool definitions, not the server's data.

source.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

stem: Your team's MCP server, named `team`, exposes a vetted `pr_review` prompt that takes a PR number. You want every engineer to run exactly that review in Claude Code instead of writing their own instructions. How do they use it?

choices.text: Reference the prompt with an @ mention, the way you attach a file or an MCP resource
choices.reason: @ mentions reference MCP resources. A server's prompts become available as commands in Claude Code instead.

choices.text: Mention a PR in the chat and wait, because Claude runs the prompt whenever one comes up
choices.reason: Claude Code lists MCP prompts as commands that you run, with arguments after the name; they aren't triggered for you.

choices.text: Copy the prompt's text into each engineer's CLAUDE.md so that it loads in every session
choices.reason: MCP prompts are discovered dynamically from connected servers, so running the server's prompt uses its vetted version directly.

choices.text: Run it as a slash command with the PR number after it, such as `/mcp__team__pr_review 456`
choices.reason: Correct: MCP prompts become commands; arguments go space-separated after the command, and the result is injected into the conversation.

takeaway: An MCP **prompt** is a vetted template run by name: in Claude Code it's a slash command that takes arguments.
explanation: MCP prompts let a server offer a vetted template that users invoke by name, so nobody has to write their own version. In Claude Code they appear as commands and take arguments such as the PR number. Choice a is tempting because @ mentions also pull in server content, but they are for resources, not prompts.

stem: A vendor's older setup guide tells you to add its remote MCP server to Claude Code over SSE. The vendor's newer docs also list an HTTP endpoint for the same server. Which should you configure?

choices.text: The HTTP endpoint: HTTP is the recommended transport for remote servers
choices.reason: Correct: HTTP is the recommended option for remote MCP servers, and the SSE transport is deprecated: use HTTP where available.

choices.text: The SSE endpoint, since SSE is the newer transport that replaces plain HTTP
choices.reason: It's the other way round: the SSE transport is deprecated, and HTTP is the recommended option for remote servers.

choices.text: A stdio entry that points at the vendor's URL in place of a local command
choices.reason: Stdio servers run as local processes on your machine; a remote server reached by URL needs an HTTP (or SSE) entry.

choices.text: Either one, since both are current and Claude Code treats them the same
choices.reason: They aren't interchangeable: SSE is deprecated, and it's meant for the services that still expose only an SSE endpoint.

takeaway: Remote server? Use **HTTP**; SSE is deprecated and is for services that offer nothing else.
explanation: Claude Code recommends HTTP for servers that don't run locally and marks SSE as deprecated. The deciding detail is that the vendor offers an HTTP endpoint, so there's no reason to stay on SSE. Choice d is tempting because both reach a remote URL, but only HTTP is the current, recommended transport.

stem: Your team wants a local stdio MCP server, started with `npx`, shared with everyone through the repo. A teammate says only HTTP servers can be project-scoped, so the team must choose between stdio and sharing it. What's right?

choices.text: The teammate is right: stdio servers are always local scope, because they run on your own machine
choices.reason: Stdio describes how Claude Code talks to the server. `--scope` is one of Claude's own options when adding a stdio server, too.

choices.text: Add it at user scope instead, which shares a server with every teammate's projects
choices.reason: User scope makes a server available across all your projects but keeps it private to your user account; it isn't shared.

choices.text: Transport and scope are separate choices, so add it over stdio with `--scope project`
choices.reason: Correct: the `--` separates Claude's own options, such as `--transport` and `--scope`, from the server's command, so stdio works at project scope.

choices.text: Convert it to HTTP first, because `.mcp.json` only accepts server entries that have a URL
choices.reason: `.mcp.json` holds stdio entries too: env-var expansion there even covers `command` and `args`, the fields a stdio server uses.

takeaway: **Transport** (how Claude Code talks to a server) and **scope** (who loads its config) are independent choices.
explanation: Transport and scope answer different questions, so any transport can be configured at any scope. The deciding detail is that the team wants sharing (project scope) and a local process (stdio) at once, which works fine. Choice a is tempting because a stdio server runs on one machine, but that's where it runs, not who loads its configuration.

stem: You use a personal note-taking MCP server in every repository you work on. Your teammates don't use it, and you don't want it written into any repo's files. Which scope should you add it at?

choices.text: Project scope, so that it's written to `.mcp.json` in each repository you open
choices.reason: Project scope writes `.mcp.json` at the repo root to share the server with your team through version control, which you don't want.

choices.text: User scope, which loads the server in all your projects and keeps it private
choices.reason: Correct: user-scoped servers are available across all projects on your machine while remaining private to your user account.

choices.text: Local scope, the default, which applies to every project on this machine
choices.reason: Local scope loads a server only in the project where you added it, so you'd have to add it again in every repository.

choices.text: Managed configuration, which deploys the server to your account everywhere
choices.reason: Managed configuration is how administrators deploy or provide servers for every user, not a place for one person's own tools.

takeaway: Personal server in every project → **user** scope; one project → local; shared with the team → project.
explanation: Scope decides which projects load a server and whether your team shares it. You need every project, which rules out local, and no sharing, which rules out project. Choice c is tempting because local is the default and sounds machine-wide, but it loads only in the project where you added the server.

stem: In repo A you ran `claude mcp add` for a Stripe server without a scope flag. It works there, but it's missing when you open repo B, and `git status` in repo A shows no new files. What explains both?

choices.text: The add failed quietly, so the server only lives in repo A's current session
choices.reason: The command did save the server, which is why it loads in repo A. Where it was saved explains the rest.

choices.text: It went to project scope, and `.mcp.json` is hidden from `git status`
choices.reason: Project scope needs `--scope project`, and its `.mcp.json` is meant to be checked into version control, so git would show it.

choices.text: It went to user scope, which reaches other projects after a restart
choices.reason: User scope would make the server available in all your projects. Without a flag, the default is local scope.

choices.text: It used local scope, saved in `~/.claude.json` under repo A's path
choices.reason: Correct: local is the default; the server loads only in that project, stays private, and is stored in `~/.claude.json`, not the repo.

takeaway: The default **local** scope is private to one project and lives in `~/.claude.json`, not in the repository.
explanation: Without a scope flag, `claude mcp add` uses local scope: one project, private to you, stored in `~/.claude.json` under that project's path. That explains both clues, the server missing in repo B and no new file in repo A. Choice b is tempting because the server is tied to repo A, but project scope would have written a `.mcp.json` that git shows.

diagram.caption: Nothing is written to the repo, and other projects don't see it.

stem: Your security team approves three MCP servers for Claude Code. Every developer must get exactly those three, and nobody may add or use any other server, including through plugins. Which control fits?

choices.text: An administrator deploys a `managed-mcp.json` defining the three servers
choices.reason: Correct: with `managed-mcp.json`, Claude Code loads only its servers (plus a few exceptions); users can't add others, plugin servers included.

choices.text: Commit the three servers to `.mcp.json` in every repository the company owns
choices.reason: By default anyone running Claude Code can connect any server they choose, so a shared `.mcp.json` doesn't stop their own servers.

choices.text: List the three servers under `managedMcpServers` so every user receives them
choices.reason: Provided servers load alongside the ones users add themselves: every user gets yours and keeps their own.

choices.text: Add each unapproved server to `deniedMcpServers` as the team discovers it
choices.reason: A denylist blocks known-bad servers and allows everything else, so a server nobody has listed yet still loads.

takeaway: A fixed, exclusive server set for everyone is **`managed-mcp.json`**; `managedMcpServers` adds servers but doesn't restrict.
explanation: The organization-wide layer is managed configuration, set by an administrator rather than a scope users pick. The deciding detail is "exactly those, and nobody may add others", which is the fixed-deployment pattern. Choice c is tempting because it also reaches every user, but provided servers load alongside users' own servers instead of replacing them.

source.title: Control MCP server access for your organization

stem: In Claude Code, you want the `github` MCP server's `create_issue` tool to run without a permission prompt, while the server's other tools keep their normal permission behavior. Which allow rule fits?

choices.text: `mcp__github`, the rule that names the server the tool belongs to
choices.reason: `mcp__github` matches any tool provided by the `github` server, so every tool on it would be allowed.

choices.text: `mcp__github__*`, which approves the server's tools one at a time
choices.reason: The wildcard also matches all tools from the server; it doesn't approve them selectively.

choices.text: `mcp__github__create_issue`, naming both the server and the tool
choices.reason: Correct: an MCP rule can name the server followed by one of its tools, and then it matches only that tool.

choices.text: `mcp__*__create_issue`, approving that tool on any server that has it
choices.reason: Allow rules accept globs only after a literal `mcp__<server>__` prefix: the server part must name a specific server.

takeaway: `mcp__server__tool` targets one MCP tool; `mcp__server` or `mcp__server__*` covers the whole server.
explanation: Permission rules can target a whole MCP server or a single tool on it. The deciding detail is that only `create_issue` should skip the prompt, so the rule must name both the server and the tool. Choice b is tempting because a wildcard looks granular, but `mcp__github__*` matches every tool on the server.

stem: Your project settings deny `mcp__github`. In your user settings you add an allow rule for `mcp__github__create_issue`, expecting the more specific rule to win. Claude still can't create issues. Why?

choices.text: User settings can't hold MCP rules, so only the project's rules are being read
choices.reason: Rules from every scope count; the catch is that deny rules from any scope are evaluated before allow rules.

choices.text: Deny rules are checked first, and an allow rule can't carve an exception out of one
choices.reason: Correct: rules are evaluated deny, then ask, then allow. The first match decides, and specificity doesn't change the order.

choices.text: Allow rules for MCP tools need a wildcard, such as `mcp__github__create_*`
choices.reason: An exact `mcp__server__tool` rule matches that one tool, so no wildcard is needed. The deny is what blocks the call.

choices.text: MCP rules must use the tool's display label rather than its `mcp__` name
choices.reason: It's the reverse: rules match canonical tool names, not the labels shown in the transcript or permission dialog.

takeaway: A server-wide **deny** beats any tool-level allow: deny, then ask, then allow, and the first match wins.
explanation: Claude Code checks deny rules before ask and allow rules, across every settings scope. The deciding detail is that the server-wide deny already matches `create_issue`, so the allow is never reached. Choice c is tempting if you think the allow was malformed, but the rule is fine; it just can't override a deny.

diagram.caption: The first match in this order decides; specificity doesn't matter.

stem: Your read-only calendar assistant reaches a calendar MCP server through the Messages API's MCP connector. The server also offers a `delete_all_events` tool. Which two `mcp_toolset` setups stop Claude from using that tool?

choices.text: Set `defer_loading: true` for `delete_all_events` in the toolset's `configs`
choices.reason: Deferred loading keeps the tool's description out of the initial prompt; the tool itself stays enabled.

choices.text: Set `enabled: false` for `delete_all_events` in the toolset's `configs`
choices.reason: Correct: a denylist. Every other tool stays enabled by default, and denylisting destructive tools suits read-only assistants.

choices.text: Keep the toolset's defaults and tell Claude in the system prompt never to delete
choices.reason: With no config every tool is enabled; the system prompt steers how readily Claude calls MCP tools but doesn't disable one.

choices.text: Move `delete_all_events` out of the toolset and into the `mcp_servers` entry
choices.reason: An `mcp_servers` entry holds connection details (type, URL, name, token); which tools are enabled is set in the toolset.

choices.text: Set `default_config` to `enabled: false`, then enable only the read tools in `configs`
choices.reason: Correct: an allowlist. Tools are disabled by default and only the ones you enable explicitly are available.

takeaway: On the API, `mcp_toolset` **allowlists** or **denylists** tools with `enabled`; `defer_loading` only delays the description.
explanation: Through the MCP connector, the `mcp_toolset` decides which of a server's tools Claude can use, with an `enabled` flag per tool or as a default for the set. A denylist and an allowlist both leave `delete_all_events` disabled. Choice a is tempting because it changes how the tool loads, but a deferred tool is still enabled.

stem: You're about to connect a dozen MCP servers to Claude Code. A teammate warns that their tool definitions will fill the context window before you type anything. With default settings, what actually loads at session start?

choices.text: Every tool's full definition, so each server should stay under a fixed tool cap
choices.reason: Full definitions are deferred by default, and Claude Code doesn't impose a fixed per-server tool cap.

choices.text: Nothing from MCP until you open `/mcp` and choose which servers to load
choices.reason: Servers connect without that step; by default, their tool names and server instructions load at session start.

choices.text: The first few servers' tools, until a set share of the context window fills
choices.reason: Threshold loading is the opt-in `auto` mode, which loads or defers all deferrable tools by total size, not by server order.

choices.text: Just tool names and server instructions; a definition loads once it is needed
choices.reason: Correct: tool search defers definitions until Claude needs them, so adding more servers has minimal impact on your context window.

takeaway: Claude Code's **tool search** is on by default: extra servers cost little context until a tool is actually needed.
explanation: Each connected server contributes tool definitions, and loading them all upfront would eat context. Claude Code avoids this by default with tool search: only names and server instructions load, and a tool's full definition arrives when Claude searches for it. Choice a is tempting if you assume everything loads upfront, but deferral is the default and there's no per-server cap.

diagram.caption: Deferred by default, so more servers cost little context.

source.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

stem: With tool search on, Claude Code defers your MCP tools. One small internal server has three tools Claude uses on nearly every turn, and the search step before each use slows things down. Your ten other servers are rarely used. What's the best fix?

choices.text: Set `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=false` so that those three tools are always visible to Claude
choices.reason: That loads every MCP tool upfront with no deferral, including all ten rarely used servers.

choices.text: Set `ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=auto` so the three tools load upfront and the rest stay deferred
choices.reason: `auto` loads all deferrable tools upfront while they total under a set share of context, or defers all of them; it doesn't pick servers.

choices.text: Set `alwaysLoad: true` on just the internal server's entry in your MCP configuration
choices.reason: Correct: that server's tools then load into context regardless of tool search, which suits a few tools Claude needs every turn.

choices.text: Set `alwaysLoad: false` on the internal server's entry so its tools are never deferred
choices.reason: `alwaysLoad: false` does the opposite: it keeps all of a server's tools behind tool search.

takeaway: Exempt only the few tools needed every turn with `alwaysLoad: true`; every upfront tool costs context.
explanation: Tool search saves context by deferring tools, but a tool Claude needs constantly pays for a search step each time. The deciding detail is that one small server is used constantly and ten are rarely used, so exempt just that server. Choice a is tempting because it removes the search step, but it loads every server's tools upfront, the cost tool search exists to avoid.

stem: Running `/context` in Claude Code shows your MCP servers using more space than you'd like, and you only use some of them. Which two steps does Claude Code's cost guide suggest?

choices.text: Disable the servers you aren't actively using, from the `/mcp` menu
choices.reason: Correct: run `/mcp` to see your configured servers and disable any you're not actively using.

choices.text: Turn off deferral so every tool definition loads once at session start
choices.reason: Definitions are deferred by default so only tool names and instructions enter context; loading them all adds more, not less.

choices.text: Move each server's usage notes into CLAUDE.md so Claude reads them upfront
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md loads into context at every session start, so those tokens are present even during unrelated work.

choices.text: Use a CLI tool such as `gh` instead of an MCP server where one is available
choices.reason: Correct: CLI tools like `gh`, `aws` and `sentry-cli` are more context-efficient because they add no per-tool listing.

choices.text: Merge all the servers into one, since each server adds a fixed context overhead
choices.reason: The guide points at per-tool listings, not per-server overhead; its fixes are disabling unused servers and preferring CLI tools.

takeaway: Trim MCP overhead by **disabling unused servers** and **preferring CLI tools** like `gh` when they exist.
explanation: Connected servers still add tool listings to context, even with full definitions deferred. The guide's two fixes are to turn off servers you don't use and to let Claude run a CLI where one exists, since a CLI adds no per-tool listing. Choice b is tempting because it sounds like a one-time cost, but loading every definition upfront uses more context, not less.

stem: You add GitHub's remote MCP server over HTTP with an `Authorization: Bearer` header, but paste the docs' placeholder instead of your personal access token. `claude mcp add` succeeds, yet `/mcp` shows the server with an ✘ and a 401. What happened?

choices.text: `claude mcp add` saved it without checking the token, and the server rejected it
choices.reason: Correct: a placeholder is accepted when you add the server, but it fails to connect later; bad credentials show an ✘ and a status such as 401.

choices.text: GitHub's MCP server only accepts stdio connections, so it refused the HTTP request
choices.reason: GitHub's MCP server is a remote server added over HTTP; the 401 says the credential was rejected, not the transport.

choices.text: The server must be added at project scope before GitHub will accept any token
choices.reason: Scope controls which projects load the server and whether it's shared; the failure here is an authentication status.

choices.text: Claude Code is about to fall back to OAuth, so wait for the browser sign-in to open
choices.reason: When a configured `Authorization` header is rejected, Claude Code reports the connection as failed instead of falling back to OAuth.

takeaway: `claude mcp add` doesn't validate credentials: check `/mcp`, and an ✘ with a 401 means fix the token you configured.
explanation: Adding a server only saves its configuration, so a placeholder token goes in without complaint. The deciding clues are the ✘ and the 401 in `/mcp`, which mean the server rejected the credential. Choice d is tempting because many remote servers sign in with OAuth, but a rejected header you configured is reported as a failure, not switched to OAuth.

stem: Your team shares the GitHub MCP server through a committed `.mcp.json`. Each developer authenticates with their own personal access token, and no token may end up in the repository. How should the shared entry pass the token?

choices.text: Paste one team token into the entry's `headers`, since `.mcp.json` stays private to each user
choices.reason: `.mcp.json` is checked into version control so the whole team gets it, so a pasted token would sit in the repository.

choices.text: Change the entry to stdio, because a server reached that way needs no token at all
choices.reason: GitHub's MCP server is remote and authenticates with a personal access token passed as a header.

choices.text: Reference an environment variable that each developer sets, as in `Bearer ${API_KEY}`
choices.reason: Correct: `.mcp.json` expands env vars in `headers`, so teams share one config while keeping sensitive values like API keys out of it.

choices.text: Have each developer re-add the server with their token using `--scope project`
choices.reason: Project scope writes to the shared `.mcp.json`, which goes into version control, so each token would land in the repository.

takeaway: Shared scope, private secret: in `.mcp.json`, reference credentials as `${VAR}` and let each developer set the value.
explanation: Project scope shares the configuration, so whatever is written in `.mcp.json` reaches everyone through git. The deciding detail is that the entry must be shared but the tokens must not, which env-var expansion in `headers` handles. Choice d is tempting because it uses a scope flag, but project scope writes the token straight into the shared file.

source.title: Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP

stem: Your `get_orders` tool queries a database. When the connection fails, your code catches the exception and sends back a `tool_result` with no content. Claude then tells a customer they have no orders. What should that `tool_result` contain instead?

choices.text: The error message in `content`, with `is_error: true`, so that Claude knows the lookup failed
choices.reason: Correct: when tool execution results in an error, return the message in `content` with `"is_error": true`. Claude then incorporates the error into its response.

choices.text: No content, but with `stop_reason` set to `tool_use` so that Claude knows to call the tool again
choices.reason: `stop_reason` is a field of Claude's response, not of your `tool_result`. An empty result is valid for a call with no output, so it hides the failure.

choices.text: A placeholder order list, so Claude has something to show the customer while the database recovers
choices.reason: Made-up data gives the customer wrong answers. `is_error: true` with the error message is how you tell Claude the tool failed.

choices.text: Nothing at all, leaving out the `tool_result` so that Claude retries the call on its next turn
choices.reason: Each `tool_use` needs its `tool_result` immediately after; leaving it out causes an error such as "tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after".

takeaway: A failed tool goes back as a `tool_result` with **`is_error: true`** and the message, never as a silent empty result.
explanation: An empty `tool_result` is how a call with no output looks, so Claude had no way to know the lookup failed and answered as if it succeeded. Marking the result with `is_error: true` and including the message lets Claude explain the failure instead. Choice c is tempting because the customer sees something, but it's wrong information.

diagram.caption: Tell Claude the tool failed; it can then explain or adapt.

stem: When your `search_flights` tool fails, it returns a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and the content "failed". Claude often can't tell users what went wrong or what to do next. What should the tool's error content say instead?

choices.text: Only the single word "error", since a shorter message keeps the conversation's context small
choices.reason: A one-word error is as generic as "failed". The page asks for what went wrong and what to try next, so Claude can recover or adapt without guessing.

choices.text: Nothing at all: send an empty `tool_result` without `is_error`, so Claude simply moves on
choices.reason: An empty result is how a successful call with no output looks, so Claude can't tell that the tool failed.

choices.text: A made-up but plausible flight list, so the user still sees results while search is down
choices.reason: Invented data gives users wrong answers. Report the failure with `is_error: true` and a useful message.

choices.text: What went wrong and what to try next, such as "Rate limit exceeded. Retry after 60 seconds."
choices.reason: Correct: the page says to write instructive error messages. Instead of generic errors like "failed", include what went wrong and what Claude should try next.

takeaway: Make tool errors **instructive**: say what went wrong and what to try next, not just "failed".
explanation: Setting `is_error: true` tells Claude the tool failed, but the message is what lets it recover or explain. Naming the problem and the next step gives Claude that context instead of leaving it to guess. Choice a is tempting because short messages save tokens, but a one-word error is just as unhelpful as "failed".

stem: Claude sometimes calls your `get_weather` tool without its required `location`. Your handler raises an exception, and your loop ends the conversation with a generic error page. What does the Handle tool calls page suggest sending instead?

choices.text: A plain user text message asking the user to type in their location again before continuing
choices.reason: The `tool_use` must be answered by its `tool_result` immediately after. The page suggests a `tool_result` that states the error so Claude can correct the call.

choices.text: A `tool_result` with `is_error: true` naming the missing parameter, so Claude can call again
choices.reason: Correct: continue with a `tool_result` indicating the error, and Claude will try the tool again with the missing information filled in, retrying 2-3 times before apologizing.

choices.text: The previous request again, unchanged, since Claude's next attempt will probably include it
choices.reason: Resending without saying what was wrong gives Claude nothing to correct; the page suggests returning the error in a `tool_result`.

choices.text: A `tool_result` with a default location filled in, so the user still gets some weather answer
choices.reason: Guessing an input hides the problem. The page suggests returning the error with `is_error: true` so Claude retries with the missing information.

takeaway: An invalid tool call is an error Claude can fix: report it with **`is_error: true`** and Claude retries with corrections.
explanation: A missing parameter is terminal for that exact call, but Claude can send a corrected one if it's told what was wrong. Returning the error as a `tool_result` keeps the conversation going and lets Claude retry. Choice d is tempting because the user gets an answer, but a guessed location gives the wrong one.

stem: Your platform team built an MCP server that only runs on the company network at `mcp.corp.internal`. Engineers keep asking where to find it, and someone proposes publishing it to the official MCP Registry so their tools can discover it like any public server. What's the right call?

choices.text: Publish it, using domain-based authentication to prove the company owns the corporate namespace
choices.reason: Namespace authentication proves who owns a name, but it doesn't change what the registry accepts, and it doesn't support servers reachable only on a private network.

choices.text: Publish only its metadata and keep the code private, since the registry never stores server code
choices.reason: The registry does host only metadata, but publishing still needs a publicly available install method or a publicly reachable server. This one is neither.

choices.text: Publish it to the official registry but mark the listing as visible to your organization only
choices.reason: The official registry is for publicly accessible servers and doesn't support private ones, so there's no way to list this one for just your organization.

choices.text: Host a private MCP registry for the company and list the server there instead of the official one
choices.reason: Correct: the registry docs say it doesn't support private servers, such as ones on a private network, and recommend hosting your own private MCP registry for them.

takeaway: The official MCP Registry is for **publicly accessible** servers; internal ones belong in a **private registry** you host.
explanation: Matching a contribution to its channel includes checking who the channel is for. The official MCP Registry catalogs publicly accessible servers, and a server on a private network such as `mcp.corp.internal` is exactly the private case it doesn't support. Choice a is tempting because proving ownership sounds like the hard part, but ownership isn't what's missing here: the server isn't public.

diagram.caption: Internal servers go in a registry you host, not the public one.

stem: Your team pushed a useful set of skills to a public GitHub repository with no license file. A partner company wants to copy and adapt them, reasoning that anything in a public repository is free to reuse. What's the situation?

choices.text: They can reuse it freely, since publishing publicly puts the code in the public domain
choices.reason: Publishing doesn't give up your rights. Without a license, default copyright law applies and you keep all rights to the code.

choices.text: They can adapt it but not redistribute it, since public repositories allow private changes
choices.reason: Others can view and fork a public repository on GitHub, but without a license no one may reproduce, distribute or create derivative works.

choices.text: Default copyright applies, so add a license stating what others may do with the skills
choices.reason: Correct: without a license, default copyright applies and no one may reproduce, distribute or create derivative works. A license tells others what they can and can't do.

choices.text: It depends on the partner's own license, which then covers anything they copy in
choices.reason: Rights to your code come from you: a software license tells others what they can and can't do with your source code, and you haven't given one.

takeaway: No license means **default copyright**: others can't reuse your code until a license says they may.
explanation: Rights come before anything else in a contribution. GitHub's licensing docs say that without a license, default copyright applies: you keep all rights, and no one may reproduce, distribute or create derivative works. Choice a is tempting because the repository is public, but public only means others can view and fork it on GitHub, not reuse it.

stem: Your plugin's helper script includes a substantial chunk of code copied from an MIT-licensed open-source project. You're about to contribute the plugin to a shared marketplace. What does the MIT license require you to do about that code?

choices.text: Nothing, since MIT is permissive and lets anyone use the code without conditions
choices.reason: MIT permits use, copying, modification and distribution, but subject to a condition: the copyright notice and permission notice stay with the code.

choices.text: Relicense the whole plugin under MIT, since any MIT code makes the project MIT
choices.reason: MIT's condition is that its notices be included in copies or substantial portions of that software; it sets no condition on the rest of your project.

choices.text: Get written permission from the original authors before including their code
choices.reason: The license already grants permission, free of charge, to anyone who obtains a copy. Its condition is keeping the notices, not asking again.

choices.text: Keep the original copyright notice and MIT permission notice with the copied code
choices.reason: Correct: MIT requires that the copyright notice and permission notice be included in all copies or substantial portions of the software.

takeaway: Permissive isn't condition-free: **attribution**, the original notices, travels with any code you reuse.
explanation: Attribution is part of the rights check that comes before technical review. The MIT license grants broad permission to use, modify and distribute the software, on one condition: the copyright notice and permission notice must be included in all copies or substantial portions. Choice a is tempting because MIT is known as permissive, but dropping the notices breaks the one condition it sets.

stem: A shared skills repository asks every contributor to sign off commits under the Developer Certificate of Origin. Part of the skill you want to contribute was first written during a customer engagement. What are you certifying when you sign off?

choices.text: That you created it, or it builds on open-source work, and you have the right to submit it
choices.reason: Correct: the DCO certifies the contribution's origin, that you created it or it builds on suitably licensed work, and your right to submit it under the project's license.

choices.text: That the maintainers have already reviewed the code and confirmed it works as described
choices.reason: Sign-off is the contributor's own statement about where the contribution came from and their right to submit it, not a record of the maintainers' review.

choices.text: That the contribution is free of bugs and security issues, so reviewers can merge it quickly
choices.reason: The DCO is about where the contribution came from and your right to submit it, not about its quality or security.

choices.text: That the contribution stays private to the project and its current group of contributors
choices.reason: The opposite: you certify that you understand the project and contribution are public, and that a record of the contribution is kept.

takeaway: Sign-off is a statement about **rights**, so settle who owns engagement code before you contribute it.
explanation: Rights and attribution come before technical review. The Developer Certificate of Origin is the contributor's certification that they created the work, or that it's based on suitably licensed work, and that they have the right to submit it under the project's license. Part of this skill came from a customer engagement, so confirm you hold that right before signing. Choice b is tempting because sign-off feels like approval, but it's about origin, not review.

stem: Your plugin's hook sends anonymous usage counts to your analytics endpoint. You're preparing the plugin for Anthropic's directory, whose security scan looks for behavior a plugin doesn't disclose. What's the best preparation?

choices.text: Minify the hook script so the scan sees less code and the endpoint isn't exposed
choices.reason: Code the scan can't read is held for a reviewer. The checklist asks for readable source, not compiled, packed or minified code.

choices.text: Say in the README what the hook sends and where, and commit readable source
choices.reason: Correct: the checklist says to describe everything the plugin runs, sends or fetches in its README and to commit readable source. Disclosure alone doesn't make a behavior allowed.

choices.text: Ship the hook switched off, then enable it in a version after the listing is live
choices.reason: The scan runs on each new commit the directory picks up, so later versions are checked too, and hiding behavior from review is what the scan looks for.

choices.text: Leave the README as it is, since anonymous counts aren't personal data
choices.reason: The scan looks for undisclosed behavior such as sending data elsewhere. The README should say what the plugin sends, whether or not it's personal data.

takeaway: Make behavior **visible**: say in the README what the plugin runs and sends, and ship source a reviewer can read.
explanation: A maintainer accepts what they can verify. The directory's security scan looks for undisclosed behavior such as sending data elsewhere, so the fix is to disclose it in the README and keep the source readable. Choice a is tempting because it seems to protect the endpoint, but minified code is exactly what the scan can't read, so the version is held for a reviewer. A complete README still doesn't make a behavior allowed: the directory policy decides that.

stem: To make your MCP-backed plugin easy to try, its README example and its `.mcp.json` both include your team's real API key. Before contributing the plugin to Anthropic's directory, what should change?

choices.text: Move the key into the README only, since documentation isn't loaded when the plugin runs
choices.reason: The checklist says to keep real credentials out of every file, documentation and examples included.

choices.text: Read the key from a variable already set in the user's environment and send that instead
choices.reason: Reading a credential already set in the user's environment and sending it to a server is held for a reviewer. Ask the user for the value instead.

choices.text: Remove the key and ask each user for their own value through the plugin's configuration
choices.reason: Correct: real credentials stay out of every file. The checklist says to ask for each value through the plugin's own configuration, marked sensitive.

choices.text: Keep the key but restrict it to read-only scopes, so a leak would cause less damage
choices.reason: Narrow scopes limit damage, but the rule is no real credentials in any file: validation blocks a plugin that ships one.

takeaway: A contributed asset ships with **no real secrets**: each user supplies their own credentials.
explanation: Once an asset is shared, everyone who installs it gets every file you ship. The directory blocks real credentials in any file, documentation and examples included, and asks for each value through the plugin's own configuration instead. Choice d is tempting because least privilege is good practice, but a restricted key is still your key in strangers' hands, and validation still blocks it.

stem: Your security team proposes a shortcut: any MCP server listed in the official MCP Registry can be approved for internal use without further review, since the registry must have vetted it. What's wrong with that reasoning?

choices.text: The registry checks who published a server and hosts metadata; it doesn't security-scan server code
choices.reason: Correct: the registry focuses on namespace authentication and metadata hosting, and delegates security scanning to package registries and downstream aggregators.

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the server's namespace is verified against a real GitHub account or domain
choices.reason: A verified namespace proves only who may publish under that name. The registry still relies on others to scan the server's actual code.

choices.text: The registry only lists servers that Anthropic built, so third-party servers never appear in it
choices.reason: Server developers can publish metadata whenever the server or its install method is publicly available. The registry isn't limited to Anthropic's servers.

choices.text: The registry runs full security reviews, but only for remote servers rather than packaged ones
choices.reason: The registry doesn't security-review any server type itself. Scanning is left to package registries such as npm and PyPI and to downstream aggregators.

takeaway: A registry listing shows **who published** a server, not that it's safe: review the code yourself or use a curated source.
explanation: Be clear about what a channel verifies. The official MCP Registry authenticates namespaces and hosts metadata, and leaves security scanning to the underlying package registries and to downstream aggregators, which can add checks and curation. Choice b is tempting because verification sounds like vetting, but namespace authentication only ties a name to its owner; it says nothing about what the code does.

stem: You forked a popular open-source plugin, added features your clients needed, and now want to list your version in Anthropic's directory. You'd like to keep the upstream plugin's name, since users already know it. What does the directory expect?

choices.text: Don't submit it, since the directory doesn't accept forks of other people's plugins
choices.reason: Forks are allowed. What the directory checks is that a fork has a name of its own.

choices.text: Keep the upstream name but add `-official`, so users know your version is maintained
choices.reason: Names that present a plugin as official are blocked, and a fork that keeps the upstream project's name is held for a reviewer.

choices.text: Keep the upstream name, since a fork carries over the original plugin's listing
choices.reason: A fork doesn't inherit a listing. A fork that keeps the upstream project's name is held for a reviewer, and a name another organization uses is taken.

choices.text: Give the fork a distinctive name of its own, separate from the upstream project's
choices.reason: Correct: forks are allowed, but the checklist says to give a fork a name of its own; a fork that keeps the upstream name is held for a reviewer.

takeaway: Forks are welcome, but a fork needs **its own name** so it can't be mistaken for the upstream plugin.
explanation: Attribution includes being clear whose work is whose. The directory allows forks but expects each to have a name of its own, holds a fork that keeps the upstream name for a reviewer, and blocks names that present a plugin as official. Choice c is tempting because users already know the name, but that familiarity is exactly why a matching name could be mistaken for the original.

stem: Your consultancy turned an engagement build into a Claude Code plugin, and every consultant should be able to install it by name and get updates. It must stay inside the firm, so its repository is private. Which distribution route fits?

choices.text: Anthropic's directory, since one listing there reaches people on every Claude app
choices.reason: The directory is a public listing: the repository can be private while you submit, but must be public before the listing goes live.

choices.text: Sending each consultant a `.zip` of the plugin folder whenever it changes
choices.reason: That suits a few people, but there's no install by name and no updates: they keep loading the copy you sent.

choices.text: Your own marketplace: a `marketplace.json` added to the private repository
choices.reason: Correct: once the marketplace file is in the repository the plugin is published, with no submission form, and a private repository makes a private marketplace.

choices.text: Anthropic's official marketplace, since Claude Code adds it for every user
choices.reason: It's a public catalog that Claude Code adds for everyone, and it doesn't take submissions through the directory portal. It can't keep one firm's plugin private.

takeaway: Pick the channel by **audience**: your own marketplace in a private repo for your group, the directory for the public.
explanation: Match the contribution to the channel built for it. The publishing guide compares routes by who can install: your own marketplace reaches anyone who can reach the repository, including a private one, while the directory is a public listing whose repository must be public before it goes live. Choice a is tempting because it reaches the most people, but reaching everyone is the opposite of what a firm-only plugin needs.

stem: You want to contribute a new skill to an open-source skills repository you've never contributed to before. The skill is written and tested. What should you do before opening a pull request?

choices.text: Read the repo's contribution guidelines and shape the pull request to fit
choices.reason: Correct: maintainers write contribution guidelines to say how they want contributions made, which saves the hassle of improperly created pull requests that must be rejected and resubmitted.

choices.text: Open the pull request now, and let the maintainers say what they want changed
choices.reason: That's the round trip guidelines exist to avoid: a pull request made the wrong way gets rejected and has to be resubmitted.

choices.text: Fork the repository and publish your copy, so the skill skips review entirely
choices.reason: A fork is your own copy, not a contribution. Nothing reaches the shared repository's users until its maintainers accept it there.

choices.text: Email the skill to one maintainer directly, so it skips the public queue
choices.reason: Going around the channel the project set up means the contribution is not made the way its maintainers asked for.

takeaway: Match the contribution to the channel: read the project's **contribution guidelines** before you open a pull request.
explanation: Contributing back means fitting a channel someone else maintains. A repository's contribution guidelines say how its maintainers want contributions made, and following them avoids pull requests that must be rejected and resubmitted. Choice b is tempting because review will surface problems anyway, but that's exactly the round trip the guidelines are there to prevent.

diagram.caption: Read how the maintainers want contributions before you make one.

stem: Your company open-sourced its MCP server and published the package on npm. You want MCP marketplaces and other aggregators across the ecosystem to be able to discover it. Which channel is built for that?

choices.text: An internal wiki page that lists the server's install command
choices.reason: A wiki page reaches only the people who find it. MCP clients and aggregators can't discover a server from it.

choices.text: The official MCP Registry, which catalogs publicly accessible servers
choices.reason: Correct: the registry is the official centralized metadata repository for publicly accessible MCP servers, and it is meant to be consumed mainly by downstream aggregators such as marketplaces.

choices.text: The npm listing alone, since the package registry already describes it
choices.reason: npm hosts the package with its code. The MCP Registry hosts the server metadata that points to that package, which is what aggregators pull.

choices.text: A private MCP registry that your company hosts for its own engineers
choices.reason: A private registry suits servers only a narrow set of users can reach. This server is public and meant for everyone.

takeaway: A public MCP server's metadata goes to the **MCP Registry**; its code stays in the package registry.
explanation: Match the contribution to the channel built for it. The official MCP Registry catalogs publicly accessible servers, holding metadata that points to the package on npm, and downstream aggregators such as marketplaces read from it. Choice c is tempting because the package is already public, but npm hosts the code, while the registry hosts the metadata aggregators pull.

diagram.caption: The package holds the code; the registry holds metadata that points to it.

stem: You're contributing a ticket-triage skill to a shared open-source repository that asks for a DCO sign-off. The skill's example cases are real support tickets you copied from a customer's system during the engagement. What should you do before signing off?

choices.text: Replace the customer's tickets with examples you wrote yourself
choices.reason: Correct: by signing off you certify that you created the contribution, or that it's based on suitably licensed work, and that you have the right to submit it. A customer's tickets are neither.

choices.text: Nothing, since the tickets are only examples and not part of the code
choices.reason: The certification covers the contribution as a whole. You'd be certifying a right to submit material that came from the customer.

choices.text: Remove the customer names from the tickets and keep the rest as it is
choices.reason: Removing names doesn't make the tickets yours. You still couldn't certify that you created them or have the right to submit them.

choices.text: Ask the maintainers to review the code first and settle the tickets later
choices.reason: A sign-off certifies your right to submit at the time you contribute. A code review can't settle whether the tickets were yours to share.

takeaway: Settle **rights** before review: material from a customer isn't yours to contribute, however useful it is.
explanation: Rights and attribution come before technical review. The Developer Certificate of Origin has you certify that you created the contribution, or that it's based on suitably licensed work, and that you have the right to submit it; it also notes that the contribution is public. Choice c is tempting because anonymizing feels responsible, but the tickets still belong to the customer.

stem: You want to contribute a skill to a community collection whose users run many different agent products, not only Claude Code. How should you package the skill so all of them can use it?

choices.text: As a long system prompt that each user pastes into their own agent
choices.reason: A pasted prompt has no metadata for discovery and sits in context in full. A skill loads its instructions only when a task matches.

choices.text: As an Agent Skills folder: a SKILL.md with metadata and instructions
choices.reason: Correct: Agent Skills are an open format, a folder with a SKILL.md holding a name, a description and instructions, so a skill built once works across skills-compatible agents.

choices.text: As a script with no instructions, since any agent can read the code
choices.reason: A bare script has no description telling an agent when to use it and no instructions for how. SKILL.md carries both.

choices.text: As screenshots of the workflow, so users can rebuild it in their agent
choices.reason: An agent can't load a screenshot as a capability. Contributors would each rebuild it by hand, and the copies would differ.

takeaway: For a skill meant for many agents, use the open **Agent Skills** format: one SKILL.md folder works across skills-compatible agents.
explanation: Match the contribution to the channel built for it. Agent Skills are an open format: a folder with a SKILL.md holding metadata and instructions, plus optional scripts and resources, built once and usable across any skills-compatible agent. Choice a is tempting because a prompt works anywhere, but it gives up discovery and the on-demand loading that skills provide.

stem: Your team wants to contribute a plugin built during a client engagement to a public open-source repository. It includes a helper adapted from an MIT-licensed library. Which two things should be settled before anyone reviews the code?

choices.text: Whether the test suite covers every one of the helper functions
choices.reason: Coverage is part of technical review, which comes after the question of whether you may contribute the work at all.

choices.text: Whether the client agreement lets you share the work done for that client
choices.reason: Correct: contributors certify that they have the right to submit the work. Code written for a client may not be yours to share.

choices.text: Whether the plugin's name is short and easy for users to remember
choices.reason: A name is a listing detail. It doesn't settle whether you have the right to contribute the code.

choices.text: Whether the adapted code meets the library license's terms, notices included
choices.reason: Correct: you can certify work based on openly licensed code only when you have the right under that license to submit it, so its conditions come with the code.

choices.text: Whether the code style matches the repository's linter settings
choices.reason: Style is part of technical review. It can't fix a contribution you weren't entitled to make.

takeaway: Before review: confirm you **may share** the work, and that reused code meets its **license terms**.
explanation: Rights and attribution come before technical review, because no review can fix a contribution you had no right to make. The DCO has contributors certify the work is theirs to submit, or is based on openly licensed work they may submit under that license. Choices a and e are tempting because they're good practice, but they belong to the technical review that follows.

stem: A maintainer reviews every contribution to a shared plugin collection and can't take any contributor's word for what a plugin does. Which two items in your submission give them something they can check?

choices.text: Eval cases they can rerun, comparing output with and without the plugin
choices.reason: Correct: build checks show how a plugin is made, not whether it helps. Comparing output with and without the plugin on real prompts shows what it adds.

choices.text: A note that your team has used it daily for months without problems
choices.reason: A claim about your own use can't be checked by someone who wasn't there. Rerunnable cases show the behavior directly.

choices.text: Readable source, so a reviewer can see everything its scripts do
choices.reason: Correct: the checklist asks for readable source instead of compiled, packed or minified code. Code the scan can't read is held for a reviewer.

choices.text: Screenshots of the best outputs it produced for your first customer
choices.reason: Hand-picked outputs show what you chose to show. A maintainer needs results they can reproduce.

choices.text: Minified scripts, so there is less code for the reviewer to read
choices.reason: Minified code is what a reviewer can't check, and the scan holds code it can't read for a person to review.

takeaway: A maintainer accepts what they can **verify**: rerunnable evals and readable source, not assurances or screenshots.
explanation: A maintainer who didn't watch you build an asset can only accept what they can check. Rerunnable cases that compare output with and without the plugin (a) show what it contributes, and readable source (c) shows what it does. Choice b is tempting because months of use sound convincing, but it's a claim the maintainer has no way to check.

stem: Before each release, your team asks Claude Code to write release notes in a fixed template, with house rules on tone and on which changes to leave out. The rules matter only at release time, and no outside system is involved. Which extension fits?

choices.text: An MCP server that returns the template and the rules whenever Claude asks
choices.reason: MCP is for connecting Claude to external services, for data or actions. A template and house rules are knowledge, which is what skills hold.

choices.text: A hook that pastes the template into the conversation at every session start
choices.reason: Hooks are for automation that must run on every matching event. These rules are needed only at release time, so loading them into every session wastes context.

choices.text: A skill holding the template and the rules, loaded when notes are needed
choices.reason: Correct: skills hold reusable knowledge and workflows, and a skill's full content loads only when it's used.

choices.text: A subagent that writes the notes, so the rules never enter any context
choices.reason: A subagent isolates work in its own context, but it still needs the rules from somewhere. Reusable instructions belong in a skill, which a subagent can preload.

takeaway: Know-how with no outside system behind it (templates, rules, procedures) belongs in a skill, not an MCP server.
explanation: The deciding detail is that nothing external is involved: the need is know-how, a template plus house rules, used only at release time. A skill packages exactly that and loads its full content only when used. Choice a is tempting because a server can return text, but MCP's job is connecting Claude to external services for data or actions, not storing instructions.

stem: You want Claude Code to open, update and close issues in your company's hosted issue tracker during a session. Today developers copy issue text in and out of the tracker by hand. Which extension gives Claude this ability?

choices.text: An MCP server for the tracker, which supplies the tools and the connection
choices.reason: Correct: MCP connects Claude to external services for data and actions, with the connection and authentication handled by the server.

choices.text: A skill that describes the tracker's screens, fields and workflows in careful detail
choices.reason: A skill adds knowledge, not access. Knowing the tracker's layout doesn't let Claude open or close an issue in it.

choices.text: A CLAUDE.md section listing the tracker's URL and your issue conventions
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md is persistent context loaded every session. It can describe the tracker, but it gives Claude no tools to act on it.

choices.text: An output style that formats each reply as an issue ready to paste in
choices.reason: An output style sets Claude's tone and response format. Developers would still copy everything into the tracker by hand.

takeaway: When Claude must read or change a live external system, reach for MCP: it supplies the tools and the connection.
explanation: The stem asks for actions in a live, hosted system: opening, updating and closing issues. That's access, and MCP is the extension that connects Claude to external services, with the server handling the connection and authentication. Choice b is the classic mix-up: a skill can teach Claude about the tracker, but knowledge alone can't change anything in it.

stem: Each Friday a teammate exports the product catalog to a markdown file inside a skill, so Claude can quote prices and stock levels. By midweek the numbers are wrong, and Claude still can't reserve stock for a customer. What should replace the export?

choices.text: A daily export into the same skill, so the file is never more than a day old
choices.reason: A fresher file still goes stale between runs, and a file can't reserve stock. Live data and actions need a connection to the system.

choices.text: Moving the catalog file into CLAUDE.md so it loads in every session
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md loads in full on every request, so this costs context all the time and is just as stale. It still gives Claude no way to act.

choices.text: A hook that re-reads the catalog file after every tool call Claude makes
choices.reason: Hooks automate actions on lifecycle events. Re-reading a stale export doesn't make it current or let Claude reserve stock.

choices.text: An MCP server for the catalog system, for live queries and actions
choices.reason: Correct: MCP connects Claude to external services for data or actions, so prices come from the system itself and reservations become tool calls.

takeaway: A skill is for knowledge that holds still. Data that changes, and actions on it, come through MCP.
explanation: Two symptoms point to MCP: the data changes faster than any export, and Claude needs to act (reserve stock), not just read. MCP provides tools and data access for an external system. Choice a is tempting because it shrinks the staleness, but a skill still holds a snapshot and still can't perform the reservation.

stem: Your team wants Claude Code to post release announcements to the team's Slack channel, following the team's message formatting rules every time. Which two pieces make up the right setup?

choices.text: A skill whose script calls Slack's web API with a token pasted into its files
choices.reason: This makes the skill own the connection and its secret. MCP gives Claude purpose-built tools for a service, with the connection and authentication handled by the server.

choices.text: An MCP server for Slack, which gives Claude a tool to post messages
choices.reason: Correct: MCP connects Claude to external services, and posting to Slack is one of the guide's own MCP examples.

choices.text: A hook that posts Claude's latest output to Slack whenever a session ends
choices.reason: A hook fires on its event without Claude deciding, so it would post at every session end, announcement or not, and it holds no formatting rules.

choices.text: A skill such as `/post-to-slack` that holds the team's formatting rules
choices.reason: Correct: a skill gives Claude the know-how to use the tool well, like the guide's `/post-to-slack` workflow with your team's formatting rules.

choices.text: A second MCP server whose only job is to return the formatting rules
choices.reason: The rules are knowledge, not an external system. Skills hold knowledge and workflows; MCP connects Claude to services.

takeaway: MCP provides the connection; a skill teaches Claude how to use it well. Many real setups need both.
explanation: The task has two halves: reaching Slack (access) and following the team's format (know-how). The features guide pairs them: MCP for the Slack connection, with authentication handled by the server, and a skill for the formatting rules, such as a `/post-to-slack` workflow. Choice a merges both into a skill with a pasted token, skipping the server that's meant to own the connection and its credentials.

stem: Your `crm-lookup` skill bundles a script that calls the CRM's API with an API key pasted into the skill's files. Security flags that every install copies the key, and the skill now handles both how to look up accounts and how to connect. What's the better split?

choices.text: Move the key into CLAUDE.md, so the skill holds only the lookup steps
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md loads in full into every session, so the key would sit in context on every request instead, and the connection still has no proper owner.

choices.text: Keep the key in the skill, but add an instruction never to show it in replies
choices.reason: An instruction in a skill is a request, not a guarantee, and the key is still copied to every install.

choices.text: Turn the script into a hook so the lookup runs before every prompt
choices.reason: A hook fires on its event without Claude deciding, so a lookup would run on every prompt, and the key problem stays exactly as it was.

choices.text: Let an MCP server own the CRM connection and auth; the skill keeps the steps
choices.reason: Correct: MCP gives Claude tools for an external system with the connection and authentication handled by the server, and the skill keeps the know-how.

takeaway: Connections and their credentials belong to an MCP server; a skill should carry only the know-how.
explanation: The skill is doing two jobs: the lookup procedure (know-how) and the connection with its secret (access). The features guide splits these: an MCP server provides tools for the external system with the connection and authentication handled by the server, and a skill teaches Claude how to use them. Choice b is tempting, but an instruction is only a request, and it doesn't stop the key being copied to every install.

diagram.caption: Today the skill carries both the connection and its secret.

stem: A developer built, and now maintains, an MCP server whose only tool returns your team's API style guide: a markdown file that changes a few times a year. Claude calls the tool before any API work. What's the better setup?

choices.text: Keep the server, and have Claude call its tool at the start of every session
choices.reason: That still runs a service just to hand back a static file, and loads it whether or not it's needed. A style guide is reference material, which skills are built for.

choices.text: Turn the style guide into a skill that Claude loads when it does API work
choices.reason: Correct: the guide lists an API style guide as a skill example. Skills hold reference material and load their full content on demand.

choices.text: Paste the whole guide into CLAUDE.md, since its content rarely changes
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md loads in full on every request and is for what every session needs. The guide says reference material Claude needs only sometimes belongs in skills.

choices.text: Wrap the server in a subagent so its output stays out of the main context
choices.reason: Subagents isolate heavy work and return summaries, but the guide would still be served by a needless server. Reference content fits a skill.

takeaway: MCP is for reaching external systems. Static reference material belongs in a skill, even if a server could serve it.
explanation: Nothing external is involved: the 'service' just returns a file that rarely changes. The features guide lists an API style guide as a typical skill: reference material whose full content loads only when Claude uses it. Choice c is tempting because the guide is stable, but CLAUDE.md loads in full on every request, and reference material Claude needs only sometimes belongs in skills.

stem: Your `weekly-metrics` skill tells Claude how to summarize CSV files that are already in the repo, and it bundles a small script that turns them into charts. A teammate says the chart step must move to an MCP server because it runs code. What's the better call?

choices.text: Move it to an MCP server, since a skill can hold instructions but not code
choices.reason: Skills can include code: the post lists a skill's contents as instructions, code and assets. Running code isn't what calls for MCP; reaching an outside system is.

choices.text: Rebuild the step as a subagent, since a subagent is the only way to run code
choices.reason: Subagents are for delegating self-contained tasks, and they aren't the only option that runs code: the post marks skills as supporting code too.

choices.text: Keep the script in the skill; nothing here needs to reach an outside system
choices.reason: Correct: skills are folders of instructions, scripts and resources, so a script fits inside one. MCP is for tool connectivity and data access, and these files are already local.

choices.text: Paste the script into the prompt each time someone asks for the weekly charts
choices.reason: Prompts are for one-off requests and are ephemeral. A procedure you'll need repeatedly, with its code, is what a skill is for.

takeaway: Running code doesn't call for MCP: a skill can bundle scripts. Reach for MCP when Claude must connect to an outside system.
explanation: The deciding detail is that the files are already in the repo: nothing outside needs reaching. Skills are folders of instructions, scripts and resources, so a chart script belongs inside one, while MCP is for tool connectivity and data access. Choice a is the tempting misconception: running code isn't the line between them, since skills can include code too.

source.title: Skills explained: How Skills compares to prompts, Projects, MCP, and subagents

stem: A team rule says Claude must never edit files in `db/migrations/`. One teammate proposes a skill that explains the rule; another proposes an MCP server with a safe-edit tool. The rule must hold every time. What does the features guide recommend?

choices.text: A hook that runs before each edit and blocks changes to that folder
choices.reason: Correct: the guide says to put guardrails in hooks. A hook that blocks the edit is enforcement; an instruction is only a request.

choices.text: A skill that explains the rule and why the migrations folder matters
choices.reason: Claude interprets a skill's instructions, so the outcome can vary. The guide calls a rule like this in a skill a request, not a guarantee.

choices.text: An MCP server with a safe-edit tool that refuses migration file paths
choices.reason: MCP adds tools for external services; it doesn't take away Claude's built-in file tools, so nothing stops an ordinary edit.

choices.text: A CLAUDE.md line marked IMPORTANT, so Claude sees it in every session
choices.reason: CLAUDE.md is always loaded, but the guide says a rule there is still a request, not a guarantee.

takeaway: When a rule must hold every time, neither a skill nor MCP fits: enforce it with a hook.
explanation: The deciding phrase is 'must hold every time'. Skills and CLAUDE.md are instructions Claude interprets, which the features guide calls requests, and an MCP server adds tools rather than taking any away. A `PreToolUse` hook runs on its event without Claude deciding and can block the edit. Choice b is tempting because a skill can explain the rule well, but explaining isn't enforcing.

stem: Your analysts wrote a solid `quarterly-report` skill: which date ranges to filter, which accounts to exclude, how to chart the results. When they run it, Claude follows the steps but says it has no way to read the sales database. What's missing?

choices.text: More detail in the skill, such as the database's table and column names
choices.reason: Knowing the schema doesn't give access. Skills teach Claude what to do with data; reaching the database in the first place is MCP's job.

choices.text: A second skill that holds a recent export of the sales tables to work from
choices.reason: A copy inside a skill is a snapshot, not access. If Claude needs to reach the database itself, that's MCP.

choices.text: An MCP connection to the database, with the skill kept for the procedure
choices.reason: Correct: MCP connects Claude to data; Skills teach Claude what to do with that data. If Claude needs to access the database in the first place, that's MCP.

choices.text: A rewrite of the skill as a longer, more detailed set of instructions
choices.reason: The skill isn't the problem: Claude is already following it. What's missing is a connection to the database, and that's MCP's job.

takeaway: If Claude can't reach the data at all, add MCP; a skill says what to do with the data once Claude can reach it.
explanation: The skill is working: Claude follows it right up to the step that needs the sales data. What's missing is access, and the Skills explained post draws the line plainly: MCP connects Claude to data, and Skills teach Claude what to do with that data. Choice a is tempting because more schema detail sounds helpful, but knowing the tables doesn't let Claude query them.

diagram.caption: The procedure is in place; the step that needs live data has nothing to call.
